Should You Actually Add AI To That? A Four-Question Audit For Product Teams

📅 2026-11-12 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2778 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Smashingmagazine

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.
  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.
  • In a recent development, A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Victor Yocco, PhD, is a UX Researcher with a focus on AI and the author of Designing Agentic AI Experiences (CRC Press, 2026), Design for the Mind (Manning, … More about Victor ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

In a recent development, A product team at a large health insurer wants to add AI that writes the full written determination for benefits appeals specialists. The technology works as specified. However, the specialists stop using it, and the ones who keep using it take longer on each case than the ones who ignore it.

In a recent development, A short evaluation with the specialists surfaces the problem fast: reading an AI-written determination carefully enough to sign it takes about as long as writing one, and the specialist also has to check for mistakes they would never have made themselves. The feature adds work to a task these people had already mastered.

Rescoping the release fixes it. A second version surfaces the policy provisions and prior decisions relevant to each appeal and leaves the writing to the specialist. The search step disappears, review time drops, and the part of the job the specialist is good at stays where it was.

The technology is identical in both versions, and the difference is which part of the task the AI handles.

Every interface change costs the user something before it pays anything back. They have to rebuild their picture of how the tool works, learn where things are now, and decide how far to trust what the AI hands them. Nelson Cowan’s review of working memory research (2001) put the limit at about four items held in mind at once. All three of those jobs draw on the same small supply.

An AI feature in an enterprise software setting requires more from the user than a redesigned menu, because it changes what they do all day. Hand the synthesis to an AI and the user becomes a checker. Give it the recommendation too, and the job shrinks to signing off. Either change costs user attention, and for people whose training is their standing at work, either one can feel like a demotion. For example, in one study, Sophia Ackerhans (2025) and colleagues found that physicians asked to sign AI-assisted decisions reported a more serious threat to their professional identity, and explanations of the AI’s reasoning raised both trust and that threat together.

It has been revealed that we can call that the break-even line. Returns to users come in three forms:.

According to recent reports, for example, an AI-powered fraud screening tool shows the errors-caught form at work, since the analyst reviews flags they would never have raised themselves, which costs attention, and the catch rate pays for it. That puts the feature above the break-even line.

It has been revealed that four questions can help your team locate the break-even line before design work starts. Each one produces a design condition the brief can act on.

In a recent development, these questions do not replace the build decision. Funding, strategy, and existing commitments all weigh on that, and four questions cannot see any of it.

Sources indicate that run through all four questions together, since no single question settles the problem alone. Do it while the feature is still a proposal, before anyone sinks weeks into design. You will also need at least one person who does the task for a living, such as a loan officer, analyst, or benefits specialist. They do not have to sit in the roadmap meeting, and a short conversation tells you where the mental effort actually sits and whether the feature would help or add work.

Count everything the task asks of the user: the thinking, the clicking, and the checking they will owe once AI is involved. Fewer clicks proves nothing on its own, because a feature can cut clicks and still leave the person working harder. Write down the cost even when it goes up, since Question 2 may find a return that pays for it.

A loan officer reading 40 financial disclosures to find the three that conflict with lending policy is thinking hard, and AI that surfaces those conflicts cuts that demand directly. Compare that with typing a loan number into a tracking system, which costs a few seconds and almost no thought. Pre-filling that field relocates the cost instead of removing it, because the officer now checks what the machine entered. Conventional wisdom says to automate the repetitive and monotonous tasks, and the pre-filled field is where that advice misfires. In this example:.

In a recent development, you can find the tasks worth automating by comparing total effort before and after. Count the checking the user inherits on the after side.

Who the user is matters as much as what the task is. One feature can clear the line for a junior analyst and fall short for a senior one. Hand a junior analyst an AI-drafted risk summary, and they gain a starting point they lack the pattern library to produce on their own. A senior analyst, however, reads that same summary against the analysis already formed in their head, spends four minutes doing it, and learns nothing.

Sources indicate that A finding like that tells you who to ship to. Scope the addition to the group it serves.

Compare the AI approach against the user’s current method, including the spreadsheets and workarounds they built for themselves. Genuine ambiguity is one reason AI comes out ahead when someone explores options, produces a starting point, or looks for patterns too numerous to spot by hand. Scale, speed, and consistency across a group of people doing the same job are three more. A fourth is catching what the current method reliably misses, which is how the fraud screening tool earns its place. The advantage disappears once the user has a practiced route to a known answer.

For example, an HR team building a succession planning tool finds the answer running both ways inside one product. Using AI to surface internal candidates whose skill combinations nobody would think to search for wins on ambiguity and scale together, since no single right answer exists and manual review of that search space would take weeks. Drafting the notification email after someone picks a candidate loses to the method already in place. The format is familiar, the writing takes two minutes, and the person sending it holds firm opinions about tone. The candidate search earns the addition. The email draft layers an interaction onto a task that runs fine without one.

The nature of the input and the shape of the output are separate decisions. A task can hold genuine ambiguity and still call for a structured visual result instead of a conversational one. Pair this audit with a modality evaluation for the output side.

It has been revealed that every AI system makes mistakes. The question is whether your user will notice. Start with how visible the error is. Then weigh what it costs when nobody catches it, and whether the user still has the skill to catch it. Question 1 asks what checking costs. This one asks whether checking is even possible.

Recent findings suggest that error visibility varies enormously, and product teams tend to estimate it badly. For example, an AI trip planner that suggests a museum on the day it closes produces an invisible error, because nothing in the output looks wrong. The traveler finds out while standing outside a locked door in Tokyo. Compare that with a suggested flight that departs before the connecting flight lands, where the contradiction sits right there on the screen.

It has been revealed that automation bias makes the invisible cases worse. Raja Parasuraman and Dietrich Manzey (2010) reviewed decades of human factors research showing that people defer to automated output even when that output is wrong, across aviation, medicine, and process control. Trust climbs fast, and rarely as a conscious decision. Once it does, people stop applying the scrutiny that would catch the mistake.

Sources indicate that map the error surface, meaning the ways this feature can be wrong, before design work starts. List the three likeliest error types. Rate each one on visibility to the user and consequence if it slips through. Any combination of low visibility and high consequence becomes a design requirement.

Show customers where the output came from and how the system produced it. That is provenance, and it is what lets trust settle at the right level. People who can see the source, the data behind it, and when it was pulled catch errors more often. Tell the traveler that a restaurant’s hours came from a page cached in March and they know what to check. A confident-sounding paragraph with no source attached leaves them guessing.

Industry observers note that letting the routine work go is a real benefit of adding AI. Nobody needs to protect a specialist’s ability to format a citation or an analyst’s ability to total a column by hand, and arguing to preserve skills the technology has absorbed wastes everyone’s time.

Still, the judgment that catches the machine’s mistakes stays exempt from replacement. That judgment makes every other delegation safe, and disuse degrades it like any other skill.

Research in radiology reveals how fast a suggestion can override a reader’s own judgment. In a 2023 experiment, Thomas Dratsch and colleagues had 27 radiologists read mammograms alongside what they were told was an AI system (a simulation created solely for the experiment). The radiologists worked through a 10-image training set where the suggested category was always correct, then 40 more mammograms with incorrect suggestions planted in 12 of them. The result indicated how incorrect AI suggestions damaged diagnostic accuracy at every experience level. The most experienced readers, averaging 15 years, assigned the correct category 82.3% of the time when the suggestion was right and 45.5% of the time when it was wrong, while the least experienced group fell from 79.7% to 19.8%. Experience softened the effect without preventing it. A year of deferring to the same system, with the judgment it replaced sitting unused, leaves a reader in a weaker position than the one these radiologists started from.

Question 3 looks at your user today. Extend the same test 12 months forward and you arrive at Question 4. Teams that answer the first and skip the second read the resulting failures as a quality problem in the model, when the cause is the human judgment they took out of daily use.

Ask whether this user could judge the quality of the output 12 months from now if the feature vanished tomorrow. When the answer is no, the design needs a mechanism that keeps verification skill in use. Periodic blind review works well and costs little, with the user forming a judgment before seeing what the AI produced. Rotating a share of cases off AI assistance does a similar job, as does a weekly comparison between machine output and a human-produced version.

Table 1 below gathers the four questions, the signals pointing each way, and the condition each one produces.

In a recent development, table 1: The AI Addition Decision Matrix. Clear answers across all four questions point toward building the feature as proposed. A poor answer on Question 1 calls for a design condition or a change in scope, unless Question 2 finds a return that covers the cost. Questions 2 and 4 work the same way without that exception. A poor answer on Question 3 can stop the build.

According to recent reports, put the conditions in the design brief, where they become project requirements. Teams reduce AI features to yes or no because roadmap reviews demand it, and that throws away everything the audit found. A feature that answers well on Questions 1 and 2 and poorly on Question 3 proceeds only with provenance built in. Write that in on day one. Requirements that arrive at the end read as polish, and teams cut polish when timelines slip.

Recent findings suggest that let’s return to the insurer scenario from our opening. The first version of the tool fails Question 1. Writing a determination takes sustained thought, and the AI that produces the draft moves that effort into verification without reducing the total. An hour with the four questions would surface that before the first version reaches design.

It has been revealed that question 2 points in the same direction. Appeals determinations follow a familiar structure, and specialists reach the answer through a practiced route. The ambiguity in the task sits earlier, in finding which provisions and prior decisions apply.

Question 3 raises the stakes. A wrong determination affects someone’s medical coverage, and an error buried in fluent prose stays invisible until the next appeal arrives. That answer produces the provenance requirement in the second version, which cites the source document and retrieval date for every provision it surfaces.

It has been revealed that question 4 explains why the second version holds up. Specialists still write every determination, so the judgment that evaluates the retrieved material stays in daily use. Keeping version one would train specialists for a year to approve text they no longer have the practice to assess.

AI-generated meeting summaries sit inside products that millions of people open every day, and the audit reaches a different answer for them.

Recent findings suggest that on Question 1, a summary removes the work of writing notes and adds the work of checking whether it attributed a decision to the right person. Total effort drops for the participant who never took notes. For the person who always took the notes and circulated them, the trade is closer, and the verification lands on them. That split is exactly what Question 1 is built to surface.

Question 2 compares the summary against someone typing while half-listening, which produces patchy notes. A summary beats that on completeness and on consistency from meeting to meeting, so the feature clears this question for most teams.

A summary that assigns a commitment to the wrong person looks exactly like a correct one, and nobody rereads the transcript to check. On Question 3, low visibility and real consequence together turn into a requirement for a linked source timestamp behind every action item.

The feature clears Question 4, and the design needs no mechanism. Nobody loses a skill worth protecting by giving up meeting notes, and the participants keep making every decision the summary records.

Two clear answers, one segment finding, and one condition. The timestamps ship with the feature, and the habitual note-taker is the segment the team checks after launch.

You can run this before the next AI feature reaches your roadmap.

According to recent reports, everett Rogers (2003) called this pro-innovation bias, the assumption that new capability means progress before anyone verifies the benefit, and competitive pressure turns a rival’s announcement into an internal mandate. An hour of structured questions gives your team a way to answer that pressure.

Recent findings suggest that audit results land badly when a designer presents them as reasons the feature should not exist. The conditions are the useful output, so bring those into the product review.

Start by naming the segment the feature serves, which makes the answer a yes for someone. Hand over the error surface as a requirement with a cost attached. A product manager can act on a request for timestamps behind every attributed decision, and nobody can act on a worry that people might not trust the output. Then offer the change in scope without waiting to be asked. A version that surfaces the provisions instead of writing the determination is a smaller build with a better adoption story, and that framing moves a roadmap conversation forward.

A sentence that works out loud: We think this clears the bar for junior analysts and adds a verification step for senior analysts, so we would scope it to onboarding and revisit the rest next quarter.

In a recent development, the attention a person can spend in a working day stays fixed no matter how good your model gets. Before the next feature reaches design, write down what it will cost the person doing the work and which of the three returns pays for it. With both answers in hand, your team can walk into the roadmap review with a scope to propose.

AI Sped Up The Build: How Can Accessibility Testing Keep Up?

  • Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Andrew Chung is Chief Product Officer at Level Access, a Leader in the first Gartner® Magic Quadrant™ for Digital Accessibility Platforms. Andrew leads the … More about Andrew ↬.

Weekly tips on front-end & UX.Trusted by 182,000+ folks.

This article has been kindly supported by our dear friends at Level Access, who help organizations create accessible and legally compliant websites, mobile apps, software, and other digital experiences. Thank you!

Lately, I’ve been thinking and writing a lot about what AI is doing to product development, and what that means for accessibility. The thing that has my wheels turning is a finding from Level Access’s 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. Basically: AI is helping us hit fast-forward on the build, but testing practices haven’t kept up.

In a recent development, we asked more than 2,500 professionals where they noticed AI was speeding up their work in the SDLC. Most said they noticed gains in planning (58%), design (61%), and development (51%). But QA and testing lagged behind: Only 30% said AI had sped up that stage.

Industry observers note that these results point to a two-speed workflow. AI has turbocharged design, planning, and development, while checking and validation are still running at a very different pace. This means a lot of teams are likely racing through the build, then being forced to hit the brakes the moment someone has to answer a pretty fundamental question: Is this thing actually accessible?

Accessibility has historically been treated as a QA bottleneck, and AI is pushing far more work into it, faster. If your team has already shifted left on accessibility, you’re off to a good start. But AI has reshuffled the workflow, so even proactive teams need to work out where those early checks belong now.

According to recent reports, this matters because right now, the web is moving in the wrong direction. WebAIM’s latest scan of the top million home pages found that automatically detected errors per home page rose 10.1% in a year, from 51 to 56.1 per page. WebAIM cited AI-assisted coding as one possible contributing factor.

Recent findings suggest that so how do we get validation out of first gear? How do we build human judgment into the workflow as AI keeps pushing the pace?

We looked at the organizations that are improving across every accessibility metric they track (a group we call the “improvers”) to find out what they’re doing differently.

Here’s what stood out: AI adoption made the smallest difference of anything we measured. Improvers use AI at a similar rate to everyone else we surveyed. Their edge indicates up in the maturity of their surrounding accessibility practices — things like training, communication, and a culture of accessibility.

According to recent reports, A quick caveat: This is survey data, so it only highlights correlation, and mature programs may simply be better at tracking and reporting their wins. Even so, this finding was hard to ignore.

Recent findings suggest that and it got even more interesting. Professionals in mature accessibility programs were nearly six times as likely to say AI helps them prioritize complications. They were also nearly three times as likely to say it helps them tackle accessibility more proactively in development.

According to recent reports, in other words, AI works best as an amplifier of a strong program. With context, testing, environments, and guardrails in place, agents can take on a large share of the work from drafting through to operations, and much of the time lost to waiting and handoffs goes away. People stay responsible for deciding what to build and for approving what ships.

So let me ask you: When it comes to accessibility, where does human judgment sit in your workflow today?

Sources indicate that not sure? Here’s a quick way to find out.

Pick a feature you shipped recently and trace it from the first Figma frame to production. Mark every moment a person decided whether it would work for someone using a keyboard, a screen reader, or their browser at 400% zoom.

In a recent development, how many marks did you get? If most of them cluster at the end of creation, you’re likely heading to one of two places: You’ll either ship accessibility barriers or spend the time you saved upstream fixing them later, when they’re harder and costlier to fix.

Here’s how to avoid both outcomes by building the right accessibility checks and judgment calls into the work your team is already doing.

As AI takes on more work, people need to stay involved at three points: finding concerns, fixing them, and documenting the evidence. Each one plugs into a step your team already takes, like a handoff, a pull request, or a review, so nothing new gets added to the timeline, and accessibility keeps pace with the work that’s in motion.

Context fades fast. Put the first judgment checkpoints as close to the creation work as you can:.

Sources indicate that found the glitch? Great. Fix it while it’s fresh. When issues end up as tickets, make sure the context travels with them. They should carry the element, the repro, the related WCAG criterion, a suggested fix, and the PR link, so context doesn’t leak.

The worst time to start gathering evidence is when somebody’s asking for it.

Recent findings suggest that every check, fix, and judgment call throughout the process described above should ideally leave a trail. A fix isn’t done until something fails if the matter comes back. Ask your AI assistant to write the regression test with the fix and put the finding link and any judgment call in the PR description. That’s the receipt.

A passing test shows a known glitch hasn’t returned. It doesn’t show the experience works. For what automation can’t cover, add a short note to the PR: what you tested, with which assistive technology, and any judgment calls you made.

AI has given digital creation a speed boost, but broadly speaking, validating the work hasn’t kept pace. Closing that gap isn’t about adopting more AI in more places or abandoning the toolset that helped make your team faster.

According to our data, the opportunity in front of teams is to build the practice around that toolset, so that human judgment is flagged, embedded, and acted on earlier, and more often.

Recent findings suggest that we’ve only scratched the surface of what our data tells us about AI and accessibility. If you’re curious about what else we found, check out the 2026 State of Digital Accessibility Report. There’s plenty more to unpack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The Stedelijk Museum in Amsterdam has unveiled that the Dutchman Krist Gruijthuijsen will take over as its new director from July 2027.

Moving from Finland, where he has since 2025 been director of the Espoo Museum of Modern Art (EMMA), he remarked he wants to bring an outsider’s perspective and a focus on how the modern city connects with the world.

It has been revealed that “The Stedelijk museum’s strength is in bringing large and Modernist exhibitions to the Netherlands,” he tells The Art Newspaper. “People go to the Rijksmuseum for Rembrandt and to the city [Stedelijk] museum to understand how Amsterdam has developed, to understand Modernism through the lens of art and design.”.

In a recent development, the Stedelijk Museum enjoyed success last year with an Anselm Kiefer show—organised with the neighbouring Van Gogh Museum—and an exhibition of work by the Dutch photographer Erwin Olaf, increasing annual ticket revenue compared to 2024 by almost a quarter, to €10.8 million. Its current Yayoi Kusama show has been extended to the end of January due to its popularity.

It has been revealed that this success stands out against a backdrop of Dutch museums reporting financial pressure and a fall in visits compared to pre-pandemic levels. The Rijksmuseum’s most recent annual report describes internal discussions that took place about the fact visitor numbers fell 4% in 2025 to 2.3 million, while the Rembrandt House Museum recently warned that rising tourist taxes will damage cultural tourism.

But Gruijthuijsen said he is more interested in variety than visitor records. “I’m not a visitor numbers director,” he indicates. “It is quality rather than quantity: what we need economically, and the rest is a plus. It is very difficult these days because people only choose what they know. My goal is first and foremost to support artists and art.”.

Gruijthuijsen takes over from Rein Wolfs, who has been the director since 2019.

From one of the first exhibitions to establish Van Gogh’s work in 1905 to experimental reveals of the 1960s, the Stedelijk Museum created an international reputation for contemporary art, which Gruijthuijsen wants to make relevant today. “The DNA of the city museum is a modern day and global perspective—trying to find connections,” he notes.

From the Finns, he will also bring an important lesson in terms of improving diversity and tackling under-represented subjects, he claims: “Less talking, more doing.”.

The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Strategy further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the Heffel Fine Art Auction House held its marquee autumn evening sales on Wednesday (18 November) in Toronto, attracting a packed house of bidders and spectators to the city’s swank Yorkville district and generating C$14.4m ($10m) in sales, works by Canadian masters taking top dollar. As things got underway, a Heffel representative noted that any US tariffs were “the responsibility of the buyer”, a reflection of these often-testy times.

“At a time of strong national pride, it is especially meaningful to see collectors celebrating Canada’s artistic achievements and our distinct national culture,” David Heffel, the auction house’s president, remarked at the end of the evening.

Heffel's evening auctions in Toronto on 18 November Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

According to recent reports, the back-to-back sales (41 lots of post-war and contemporary art followed by 47 works of Canadian, Impressionist and modern art) got off to a flying start when a watercolour by the Vancouver-born artist E.J. Hughes hammered for C$475,000 ($331,700)—nearly 12 times its high estimate. Titled Wharves at Chemainus (2000) and depicting the titular logging community on Vancouver Island, the painting is modest in size at 20in by 24in; with fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900).

Sources indicate that hughes had made waves at Heffel’s auctions last spring, when his Coastal Boats Near Sidney, BC realised a whoppingC$5.7m ($4.1m), including fees. Several more Hughes works were up for sale Wednesday night including two that significantly outperformer their estimates: The Hope River at Chilliwack, BC (1961), which took in C$253,250 ($176,800) with fees; and The Freighter “World Ares” at Crofton (1980), which hauled in C$229,250 ($160,000) including fees.

Emily Carr, Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure), around 1912 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

Sources indicate that the second sale’s cover lot, Emily Carr’s luminous canvas Alert Bay (with Welcome Figure) (around 1912), brought C$1.3m ($922,000) including fees, comfortably within its estimate. It was the only seven-figure result of the night. Some of the proceeds from its sale will benefit the Audain Art Museum in Whistler, British Columbia, where it was shown in the context of a major traveling exhibition of Carr’s work in 2019-20.

In a recent development, A work on paper by the Carr, Music in the Trees (around 1935), topped its high estimate to achieve an impressive C$421,250 ($294,100) with fees. In all, six works by the Victoria-born artist were sold at Heffel on Wednesday night, fetching a combined, fee-inclusive total of C$2.5m ($1.7m).

Jean Paul Riopelle, Herbeuse, 1967 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

A handful of works by Jean Paul Riopelle were on offer during the post-war and contemporary portion of the night, generating around C$1.3m ($907,800) in sales. His large-scale, wintry abstraction Herbeuse (1967),proved particularly appealing. Swift bidding pushed it to around double its high estimate. With fees, the price came to C$571,250 ($398,900). It was shown in the Carnegie International the year Riopelle painted it, and later in Paris, where the Montréal-born artist, a master of the palette knife, spent decades. The work with the highest estimate in the post-war and contemporary sale, Riopelle’s Brumaire (1953), was expected to bring between C$1.5m and C$2m, but failed to sell.

It has been revealed that among the night’s other massive-ticket items was Paul-Émile Borduas’s oil painting Empâtement (1957), from the artist’s black-and-white period—and punctuated with splashes of red. It realised C$841,250 with fees ($587,400), easily topping its high estimate of C$500,000. It had been acquired directly from the artist by London’s Arthur Tooth & Sons gallery in 1957 and, more recently, was in the collection of Québecois lyricist and songwriter Luc Plamondon.

Paul-Émile Borduas, Empâtement, 1957 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

J.E.H. MacDonald’s oil sketch Magnetawan River Rapids (1912), a preparatory work for a major canvas that is in the collection of the Art Gallery of Hamilton, achieved C$451,250 with fees ($315,000), tripling its high estimate of C$150,000.

According to recent reports, arguably the surprise of the night was Ivan Eyre (1935-2022), who was long a professor at the University of Manitoba and is best known for his prairie landscapes. His intensely autumnal acrylic-on-canvas landscape Golden Rod (1981) realised C$391,250 with fees ($273,200), more than tripling its high estimate of C$120,000 while setting a upcoming auction record for the artist. That record was smashed in turn just one lot later, when Eyre’s Yellow Wood (around 1995) realised C$481,250 with fees ($336,000), five times its high estimate of C$90,000.

Ivan Eyre, Golden Rod, 1981 Courtesy Heffel Fine Art Auction House.

The beloved William Kurelek, who was raised on a farm near Winnipeg, also made a splash.His snowy landscape painting I Knew How the Clouds Arise (1969), which was featured on the cover of the catalogue for the artist’s first retrospective in 1970, realised C$313,250 including fees ($218,700), just over its high estimate, while the evocative campfire scene Wiener Roast on My Father’s Farm (1974), exceeded expectations to sell for C$265,250 with fees ($185,200).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Wrapping up this autumn’s week of marquee evening sales in Fresh York, Christie’s 21st-century auction on Thursday (19 November) proved rather lacklustre, bringing in $117.7m ($145.9m with fees). That tally fell short of Christie’s pre-sale expectations, which do not account for fees, and projected a total take in the range of $126m to $192m. It was also a lower result compared to the auction house’s last two equivalent sales in New York—namely the $132m ($162.6m with fees) generated across 42 lots last May, and the $99.5m ($123.5m with fees) brought by 45 lots one year ago.

Recent findings suggest that just five of the 56 lots offered Thursday night failed to sell, for a slim buy-in rate of 9%. Two lots were withdrawn at the last moment, including a Jeff Koons sculpture estimated to bring between $3m and $5m. Twenty-four lots were backed by third-party guarantees and nine were backed fully by house guarantees, representing around 59% of all the works offered. Auction records for three artists were broken over the course of the night.

Roy Lichtenstein, Small Wall Explosion, 1965 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Business began with a bang at Christie’s Rockefeller Center salesroom: the first lot was Roy Lichtenstein’s Small Wall Explosion (1965), executed in porcelain enamel on steel and perforated steel relief to mimic the Ben-Day dot style from his paintings. It sold to a telephone bidder for $625,000 ($800,000 with fees). From an edition of six, it hailed from the collection of Antonio Homem Sonnabend, the adopted son of the late and legendary dealer and collector Ileana Sonnabend (1914-2007) and who ran his mother’s namesake gallery in its waning years. Antonio Homem died earlier this year, at age 86.

According to recent reports, another of the 19 Sonnabend lots from Sonnabend, Ashley Bickerton’s expansive wall relief Commercial Piece #3 (1990), covered with gallery and fashion-house logos and comprised of anodised aluminium, wood, leather, acrylic and rubber, sold for $120,000 ($153,600 with fees). Both the Lichtenstein and the Bickerton were backed by third-party guarantees.

Andy Warhol, Campbell's Soup Can (Turkey Noodle), 1962 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Recent findings suggest that price points for the Sonnabend trove zoomed higher with Andy Warhol’s iconicand hand painted Campbell’s Soup Can (Turkey Noodle) (1962), which sold for $7.3m ($9m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. Another Lichtenstein, the painting Large Spool (1963)—a razor-sharp depiction of the titular object that has been featured in multiple gallery and museum exhibitions—squeaked by on the tails of a third-party guarantee at $7m ($8.6m with fees) against an ambitious estimate of $10m to $15m.

It has been revealed that still in the Sonnabend lots, Jeff Koons’s toy-like Hulk (Friends) (2004-12), in polychromed bronze and standing nearly 6ft tall, found a latest home for $3.3m ($4.1m with fees). And another Warhol, redolent with Hollywood celebrity, The Kiss (Bela Lugosi) (1963) in silkscreen ink on white paper, sold to another telephone bidder for $3.3m ($4.6m with fees).

Sources indicate that A petite Jasper Johns oil painting on cardboard, Numbers (1957), measuring just 8.5in by 6in and rich in shades of grey, made $2.6m ($3.2m with fees). It was featured in the artist’s first solo exhibition at the Leo Castelli Gallery in 1958. Ileana Sonnabend acquired it from the Castelli Gallery in 1959, the same year of her divorce from Leo Castelli.

The Sonnabend group of 19 lots, including three examples of vital 20th-century French decorative art—among them a Jean Prouvé Trapéze table from around 1956 that hit $1.3m ($1.6m with fees)—all in tallied $33.3m ($41.9m with fees), compared to Christie’s pre-sale expectations for the group of $35m to $55m.

Illustrious consignor names continued with works from the collection of the late Museum of Modern Art trustee and patron Agnes Gund sold to benefit the Gund Art Foundation. They included Robert Ryman’s immaculate, small, square all-over white composition Untitled (1961), which brought $2.9m ($3.6m with fees). Vija Celmins’s photorealist oil painting Untitled (Ocean) (1990), which featured in the San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s traveling retrospective in 2018-2020, went for $5.7m ($7.1m with fees) against an estimate of $6m to $8m. It also was backed by a third-party guarantee.

Vija Celmins, Untitled (Ocean), 1990 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

In a recent development, gund acquired Alexander Calder’s hanging metal mobile The Eye in the Black (1963) from the Perls Galleries in Fresh York in in 1967. On Thursday night it went to an online bidder for $2.8m ($3.5m with fees). Cindy Sherman’s Untitled Film Still #5 (1977), also widely exhibited and written about by major critics, sold for $320,000 ($409,6000 with fees). Gund had acquired it at Sotheby’s New York in November 2000 for a hammer price of $75,000.

Gund’s contemporary taste bordered on the encyclopaedic, as evidenced by an early Robert Rauschenberg work, Untitled (Gold Painting) (1953), in gold leaf on fabric and paper collage on canvas. The diminutive work, at 8in by 8in, fetched a sizeable sum, $1.7m ($2.1m with fees). Gund acquired it at Sotheby’s in New York in May 1994 for a $55,000 hammer price.

A modestly scaled Lichtenstein work on paper in coloured pencil, graphite and paper collage, Artist’s Studio with Model (Study) (1974), sold to the art adviser Ralph DeLuca for $950,000 ($1.2m with fees).

Jim Nutt, Loom, 1999 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

A standout from the Gund trove, a work she described as “my Mona Lisa”, was another modestly-scaled work, by Jim Nutt, founder of Chicago’s Hairy Who group. Titled Loom (1999) and measuring 15in by 14in, the portrait of a woman with a penetrating gaze set a new auction record for Nutt’s work when it more than doubled its high estimate of $350,000 and ultimately sold for $850,000 ($1m with fees). The ten lots sold to benefit Gund’s charitable foundation tallied $20.3m ($25.7m with fees), squarely within Christie’s pre-sale estimate of $16m to $24m.

Though not part of the Gund Art Foundation offerings, Alice Neel’s double portrait David and Catherine Saalfield (1982) hailed from Agnes Gund’s family and brought $1.6m ($2m with fees). Gund acquired it directly from the artist the year it was painted—not surprising since the sitters were her young adult children.

Alice Neel, David and Catherine Saalfield, 1982 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Industry observers note that the appeal of buying a piece of the legacy of storied dealers and collectors did not fare so well for a work that had belonged to the late gallerist Marian Goodman. Bidding on Gerhard Richter’s Abstraktes Bild (1990) stalled at $5.7m, against an estimate of $6m to $8m, and the lot failed to sell. As Richter’s longtime New York dealer, Goodman acquired the lushly surfaced squeegee painting directly from the artist and exhibited the painting in a gallery group show the year it was made. (A second Richter from another consignor fared better, with that somewhat larger Abstraktes Bild from 1991 bringing $7.6m, or $9.4m with fees.).

Among the works from more anonymous consignors, Richard Prince’s famous Nurse series made a splash when Everglade Nurse (2003), executed in acrylic and inkjet print on canvas, sold for $3.1m ($3.9m with fees). It last sold at Sotheby’s Newly introduced York in November 2008 for $3.4m with fees, a rather flat return after 18 years.

It has been revealed that large-scale paintings destined to test living room wall space were also in evidence with Christopher Wool’s untitled black-and-white abstraction from 2009, measuring more than 8ft tall. It brought $2m ($2.5m with fees). George Condo’s more than 9ft-wide Double Heads in Blue and Silver (2014), realised $2.4m ($3m with fees). The Condo hailed from the collection of Stefan Edlis and his wife Gael Neeson, who donated 44 works cumulatively valued at more than $400m to the Art Institute of Chicago in 2015.

The top lot of the evening, unsurprisingly, was Jean-Michel Basquiat’s quirky and text-rich composition, Untitled (Leonardo and his Five Grotesque Heads) (1983), which hammered to another anonymous telephone bidder for $28m ($32.8m with fees) against a sky-high estimate of $30m to $50m.

Jean-Michel Basquiat, Untitled (Leonardo and His Five Grotesque Heads), 1983 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Evidently inspired by Leonardo da Vinci’s 1493 pen-and-ink drawing on paper A man tricked by Gypsies (also known as Five grotesque heads), from the Royal Collection Trust at Windsor Castle in London, Basquiat’s freestyle interpretation in oil stick and acrylic against a burnt orange background crackles with the artist’s terse way with wordplay and actually features eight heads in all.

Measuring 80in by 80in, the painting has no exhibition history, at least none acknowledged in Christie’s online catalogue entry—though it was included in the Whitney Museum of American Art’s 1992 Basquiat retrospective. The catalogue entry for the Whitney exhibition listed the owner as Zurich’s Bruno Bischofberger, an early and key champion of the artist. It last sold at auction at Sotheby’s London in October 2005, when it was the top lot at £736,000 ($1.3m) including fees against an estimate of £400,000 to £600,000. Sotheby’s at the time identified the buyer as “US Trade” and the current consignor acquired it from that entity in 2006.

Julia Jo, One Fell Swoop, 2026 Courtesy Christie's Images Ltd.

Sources indicate that the evening ended on a sweet note with Julia Jo’s large-scale abstraction One Fell Swoop (2026), donated to benefit the Fresh York-based Coalition for the Homeless. It set a new auction record for Jo’s work, fetching $320,000 ($409,600 with fees). (The night’s other new auction record was for the work of the Spanish artist Antonio Santín.).

Recent findings suggest that apart from that feeling, the outlook was not as rosy. “It’s been a very long week, with a lot of art, and I think people are tired,” DeLuca remarked. “The theme of the week is that estimates are a little aspirational.”.

The long week’s last burst of activity will be a pair of day sales at Christie’s on Friday (20 November), after which the US art industry will mark a pause to observe Thanksgiving before migrating south for Art Basel Miami Beach.

Tech Report: The Filmmakers Behind ‘Primetime’ Printed the Entire Movie on 16mm and Rescanned It

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Primetime, a feature film about Chris Hansen and his hit TV show To Catch a Predator, keeps viewers gripped not just by the intense story brought to life by actors Robert Pattinson and Merritt Wever, but by the striking cinematography.
  • One of the biggest reasons for its distinct filmic look is that director Lance Oppenheim and cinematographer David Bolen opted to shoot the majority of the movie on an Alexa 35 before printing it onto a 16mm Kodak 50D and rescanning it to 6K, a process known as digital-to-film-to-digital.
  • Writing for American Cinematographer, Bolen explains that he shot most of the film at 6400 ISO to “add as much noise and texture as I could.”.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Primetime, a feature film about Chris Hansen and his hit TV show To Catch a Predator, keeps viewers gripped not just by the intense story brought to life by actors Robert Pattinson and Merritt Wever, but by the striking cinematography.

One of the biggest reasons for its distinct filmic look is that director Lance Oppenheim and cinematographer David Bolen opted to shoot the majority of the movie on an Alexa 35 before printing it onto a 16mm Kodak 50D and rescanning it to 6K, a process known as digital-to-film-to-digital.

Writing for American Cinematographer, Bolen explains that he shot most of the film at 6400 ISO to “add as much noise and texture as I could.”.

Sources indicate that the crew used London-based Cinelab, which has a third-generation 16mm Cine-Mitchell recorder built in-house. Once the film print was created, it was scanned back into digital using an Arriscan, which delivers “perfect edge-to-edge focus.” The resulting footage was then regraded.

“Primetime is also a period film, in a way, and working with the film print helped make the visuals far more immersive,” says Bolen. “Any feeling of artifice in the image seemed to disappear after printing to film.”.

However, the film wasn’t shot entirely with the digital-to-film-to-digital method: Oppenheim and Bolen utilized a few obscure, frankly bizarre, cameras as they searched for a way to recreate that early 2000s aesthetic and also communicate the plot to the audience.

Sources indicate that one such camera was a 2005 MiniDV camera, the Panasonic AG DVX 100B. Bolen used this for the hidden camera shots, and it is a very similar technology that was used to film the original show, To Catch a Predator.

Industry observers note that “These cameras are a challenge, because unlike modern cinema cameras, they can’t shoot in a LOG color space,” Bolen says. “We didn’t really alter their baseline settings; we decided to lean into the cameras’ built-in contrast. To Catch a Predator has such a strong look, and we tried to match it as closely as possible in-camera. Even in the final grade, we made very few adjustments.”.

Industry observers note that but that distinct look posed a problem in the editing room: how to blend the shots taken by different cameras together. After all, DV cameras are not cinematic.

Recent findings suggest that “We couldn’t get them to match,” states Bolen on the Mark Bone YouTube channel. “Like, no matter what we did with the settings, some would skew red, some would skew green, on some the exposure seemed off.”.

Sources indicate that but Oppenheim didn’t care and threw the rules out of the window. In fact, he would film the same scenes on different cameras, and then in the edit, choose whichever one he liked.

Speaking of other cameras, there were two more that Oppenheim and Bolen used: a Plumbicon tube camera and a medical camera — the kind used for colonoscopies.

Archer Green points out that the Plumbicon tube camera actually dates back to the 1980s.

Sources indicate that “It was meant to serve as a ‘spiritual’ camera rather than a period-accurate one,” Bolen writes for American Cinematographer. “These cameras use vacuum RGB tubes that split light into red, green, and blue, and the beautiful thing is that the tubes age and burn out over time. In a way, it’s a camera that feels like it has a soul — it decays over time, just like a human does.”.

The creators of ‘PRIMETIME’ explain how they shot a scene using a 480p colonoscopy camera 🎥🤯https://t.co/Z8m4aT7YM0.

— Complex Pop Culture (@ComplexPop) September 27, 2026.

It has been revealed that for one of the close-ups of Pattinson, Bolen used a doctor’s colonoscopy camera. The crew even built a rig to hammer home the effect.

“That was a scary one because that camera does shoot 480p and I was like, ‘How am I going to get this approved?’ But to A24’s credit [the film distributor], they were like, ‘this is awesome’,” Bolen says.

It has been revealed that “There are no rules. We don’t have to shoot 6K. 480p looks awesome on the massive screen; I love it. It’s my favorite part of the movie.”.

#57368. Industry News: Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 3m • 📚 Deep Dive (697 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Five Ethiopian artefacts restituted in London ceremony

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (697 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November).
  • McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art.
  • Sources indicate that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, five historic Christian artefacts were restituted to the Ethiopian Heritage Authority in a ceremony at the country’s London embassy on Wednesday (18 November). The process was part of a wider initiative by the American collector Robert McCarthy and the Toledo Museum of Art in Ohio that is expected to see many more objects returned to Ethiopia.

McCarthy, an American financier who used to live in London and now resides in East Asia, has long been a serious collector of European medieval art. He broadened his collection in the 1990s to include Ethiopian art, at a time when there was less concern about provenance. In 2023-24 he lent objects to the exhibition Ethiopia at the Crossroads, which was presented in venues in Baltimore, Salem in Massachusetts and Toledo. It was at Toledo that he began discussions with Sophie Ong, assistant director of strategic initiatives, about the future of his collection.

Sources indicate that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

This eventually led to the new, complex arrangement. Toledo will acquire McCarthy’s 375 Ethiopian objects, one of the largest such private collections. Two thirds will be donated and the remainder bought. Some of this material will be exhibited when the museum’s galleries reopen in autumn 2027 after a major reinstallation of its permanent collection.

According to recent reports, the museum then intends to return much of the collection to Ethiopia, in tranches over the next 20 years. Any items deemed to have left Ethiopia illegally or inappropriately will be restituted. Details have not been released, but it is assumed that this will include looted material seized by British troops at the 1869 battle of Maqdala and which later came onto the international art market.

Objects judged to have been exported properly will remain at the Toledo museum. Stewardship of items with an indeterminate status will be decided jointly by the Toledo museum and Ethiopian officials. It is thought that ultimately half of McCarthy’s 375 items may be returned.

The unusual tripartite arrangement between McCarthy, the Toledo museum and the Ethiopia authorities could prove to be a template for dealing with restitution claims by other African countries. At the handover, Alula Pankhurst, speaking on behalf of the Ethiopian Heritage Authority, described it as “a newly introduced model of partnership”.

This week’s restitution of five objects to the government’s Ethiopian Heritage Authority is slightly different, in that they have been directly returned by McCarthy. The Toledo museum was unwilling to accession them because of records suggesting that they had left Ethiopia after the 1970 Unesco convention.

According to recent reports, the items are two 15th-century illuminated manuscripts and three processional crosses. All are believed to have been improperly removed from Ethiopian churches.

According to recent reports, the earliest of the two manuscripts is a Book of Revelation with a Horologium (daily cycle of prayers). It includes seven full-page illuminations, dating from around 1400. The volume was recorded in the late 20th century as being in the Saqqā Madḫānē Ālam Church in Šawā Province.

The other manuscript is a large mid-15th century Gospels, which includes full-page images of the Four Evangelists. The scholar Diana Spencer noted in a 1974 article that she saw it at the church of Emmaus Giyor near Wafa Yasus.

It has been revealed that ethiopian Heritage Authority, Addis Ababa. Photo: Stephen Chung for Toledo Museum of Art and Embassy of Ethiopia.

The three brass processional crosses being returned date variously from the late-18th to early-20th centuries. Each has incised inscriptions which may make it possible to determine which church they came from.

The five returned objects are now being sent from London to the National Museum of Ethiopia in Addis Ababa, where a newly introduced display of restituted material is scheduled to open in December. Most of the rest of the display will be material which had been looted at Maqdala.

However, the forthcoming Addis Ababa display may feed into a debate over whether religious items that can be identified with a particular location should be retained in the National Museum or returned to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.

#57367. Branding: Zero 10 brand identity by Saffron

📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Abduzeedo ↗ Open Full Page

Branding: Zero 10 brand identity by Saffron

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (435 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Abduzeedo

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.
  • In a recent development, the mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point.
  • The type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Saffron builds the Zero 10 brand identity for Art Basel from Malevich's 1915 0,10 show, a frame-like mark for digital art.

In a recent development, the mark itself does almost nothing, and that is the point. Two numerals, a round zero and a straight ten, sit far apart, open space held between them. The space is the frame: whatever sits inside it, a glowing orb, black liquid, purple fur, becomes the artwork, while the numerals stay fixed at the edges. On deep magenta, the word Future fills the width in cream capitals under a small 0 10. On black, Art creators does the same work over silver bubbles. The system frames the art, labels it, and gets out of the way.

The type is a heavy geometric sans, set large enough that single words carry a whole poster. Future, Art creators, and The collectors each run at a scale where the letterforms read as shapes first and words second, with the small 0 10 lockup above them. Every layout follows the same grid: mark at the top, one headline in the middle, the Art Basel wordmark anchored low, and artwork inset in a free corner.

Spacing does as much work as the letters. The open gap between zero and ten is protected in every lockup, and the headlines sit on broad magenta, black, or pale blue fields. Even the flags keep the discipline: one black flag carries the numerals running down its length, the next the Art Basel wordmark, so the pair reads as one system at a distance.

The identity lives on fabric, glass, and screens. Four flags run the system against a flat blue sky: purple pixel weave, black with the white numerals, soft pink, and black with the Art Basel wordmark. At the fair, the mark frames vast LED walls of particle fields and glitch color. The platform debuted at Art Basel Miami Beach, where Saffron notes the first preview day alone brought seven-figure blue-chip sales, with several collections sold out.

Saffron built the launch as a toolkit as much as a look, with messaging for every stage of the journey, to attract, educate, and convert fresh audiences. The name travels: Zero 10 reads the same in any language, and the platform now runs across Art Basel's global fairs. Some case-study imagery was generated with AI, Saffron notes. Art Basel chief executive Noah Horowitz notes the partnership "gave us the creative space to experiment and the insight to build a platform that deeply engages our community with absolute authenticity.".

See the full Zero 10 case study from Saffron.

  • Industry observers note that “On the outer screen, we’ve added a few new modes, including a viewfinder preview and flash-fill.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Halide has announced version 3.4, much of which focuses on optimizations for the iPhone Duo. This includes a new “XL” mode that is designed for two-handed operation, as well as a feature that doesn’t avoid the crease, but instead embraces it.

Version 3.4, which is available starting today, promises to maximize the viewfinder when the iPhone Duo is unfolded. Halide says this feature, called XL mode, allows for “powerful two-handed operation.”.

Industry observers note that “On the outer screen, we’ve added a few new modes, including a viewfinder preview and flash-fill. In low-light, the latter gives you a softer alternative to the built-in flash,” Halide adds.

Industry observers note that “While apps like Apple’s own camera app expand the viewfinder to take up the full screen, it’s impossible to do this without obstructing your shot with camera controls. That poses a challenge when composing shots, so we’ve taken the approach of keeping the viewfinder clean.”.

Beyond just making these changes that take advantage of the two form factors the Duo offers, Halide went one step further and specifically engineered an interface for when the Duo is half-folded. The tech giant states that while most are avoiding the crease that appears when the phone is folded, it went the opposite way and embraced it.

“Back when the iPhone X launched in 2017, we were the first app to ’embraced the notch’ by putting histograms in the ears of the phone. Today, we think we’re the first app to ’embrace the crease,’ placing the histograms in the fold, an otherwise no-man’s-land of interactions,” Halide says.

Recent findings suggest that by default, Halide’s camera controls sit on the same side as the camera itself. Tapping the arrows in the sidebar, the left and right sides swap, turning Halide into a waist level viewfinder.

Halide provided a few sample images taken with the updated Duo app:.

Halide usually doesn’t take long to enhancement its app when upcoming hardware lands, and even though the interface for this Duo-specific update feels like it should have taken a lot longer, it really isn’t too far off from what Halide provided for Apple’s iPhone 18 Pro launch. When it dropped version 3.2, which gave support for variable aperture control, that arrived on October 2, which is about three weeks after the iPhone 18 Pro landed on store shelves. This update for the Duo comes just shy of a month after the Duo launched on October 23.

Halide version 3.4 is available starting today.

ACDSee Photo Studio has declared version 27, which brings a bunch of new features, including several powered by AI, perhaps elevating the tool to the level of Adobe’s offerings.

Version 27 of the photo management and editing software for macOS introduces generative AI tools for creating and editing images, along with AI-powered organization that the manufacturer says can find and group photos together by how they look. The bulk of the updates to version 27 are AI-focused, with the top-billed new feature having the highest chance of being the most controversial: image generation.

In a recent development, “Turn a text prompt into an image, choose a preset visual effect, or bring in reference images to guide character, style, and composition, right inside the photo workflow,” ACDSee indicates. AI generation isn’t new for photography tools, as Photoshop has had it for years now, but it’s not necessarily something that photographers are specifically asking for in a Lightroom competitor. Still, it’s here now.

Sources indicate that ACDSee appears to be following Adobe’s lead with the next feature, as it now supports editing via prompting. Photographers can describe a change in plain language or “use reference images to guide the look, and reshape a photo without a single brush stroke.”.

The AI search tool looks to be an alternative to Excire Photo and will find photos visually related to any primary target, with no keywords or tagging required. Images can also be grouped by similarity.

ACDSee Photo Studio for Mac 27 is available for $119.99, including 10,000 AI Credits for generative AI tools and 100GB of cloud storage.

#57361. This iPhone App Lets You Take Photos By Clapping

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 2m • 📖 Standard (391 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Petapixel ↗ Open Full Page

This iPhone App Lets You Take Photos By Clapping

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (391 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A new iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.
  • HyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment.
  • According to recent reports, meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A new iPhone camera app, HyperCam Trigger, aims to make it easier for mobile photographers to nail the perfect action shot, group portrait, or lightning photo.

HyperCam Trigger uses various listening and detection methods to fire the iPhone’s camera at the right moment. For example, when photographing sports, children, or pets, the app can trip the shutter as soon as motion appears in the frame.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, for group portraits, which typically rely on a self-timer, HyperCam can listen for someone in the frame to clap, triggering an immediate shot. People can customize the sensitivity for the app and the delay between detection and shooting.

The app’s original purpose, which remains a core focus, was to make it easier to photograph lightning. It can use sound for this as well, though thunder arrives well after the flash of lightning itself. The app can also trigger a shot when it detects a sudden surge of light hitting the camera.

HyperCam can also trigger the shutter under other conditions, including camera shake, such as when the iPhone moves or tilts, or complete stability, such as when it is mounted on a tripod. Additionally, it can capture timelapse photos when it detects changes in light or motion, or wait to fire until someone in the frame smiles.

Lightning triggers are not a newly introduced concept in photography. Photographers with DSLRs and mirrorless cameras have been using them for years, and new ones hit the market every so often, like the Bolt Hunter earlier this year.

Lightning triggers rely on the same principle as HyperCam: it is simply impossible for a photographer to manually press the shutter fast enough to catch fleeting events like lightning. Photographers can certainly try and can improve their odds by firing off long, rapid bursts of frames. However, assistance is required for consistent success.

HyperCam Trigger is available now in the App Store for free.

In a recent development, however, some features are locked behind a paywall, including subject filters, short event video recording with frame extraction, detection zones, longer pre-trigger buffers, longer bursts, RAW recording, HDR, and more. HyperCam Pro is available for $3.99 per month, $22.99 per year, or $44.99 for lifetime access.

Apple’s Camera and Photo Software Lead Jon McCormack Has Retired

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (497 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Petapixel

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired.
  • Bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October.
  • Enhancement 11/20 @ 8 AM: McCormack shared this story on his Instagram, perhaps subtly confirming its accuracy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that jon McCormack, Apple’s head of photography and camera software development, has retired. A spectacular photographer in his own right, McCormack is stepping away, and his departure signals a major change for Apple regardless of the circumstances.

Bloomberg reports that McCormack retired at the end of October. This information has not been independently verified, as at the time of publication, neither Apple nor McCormack has confirmed his departure.

Enhancement 11/20 @ 8 AM: McCormack shared this story on his Instagram, perhaps subtly confirming its accuracy.

Sources indicate that mcCormack, who was Apple’s vice president of camera and photo engineering, has been a major figure at the Silicon Valley giant since he arrived there in 2018. He oversaw the development of not only the iPhone camera system but also the camera software and all of the computational features that go along with it.

He was present for every briefing and discussion about the iPhone camera system through that time and became personally known to everyone at PetaPixel. He is also regularly quoted speaking about Apple’s philosophy regarding cameras and photography.

“Here’s our view of what a photograph is: The way we like to think of it is that it’s a personal celebration of something that really, actually happened,” he told PetaPixel back in 2024, just as generative AI was beginning its steady march into the creative industry. Apple has, since then, largely stayed that course.

Recent findings suggest that perhaps most importantly, McCormack is actually a photographer. In April, PetaPixel featured his most recent book, titled “Patterns: Art of the Natural World.”.

“I grew up on a farm in the Outback, Queensland in Australia,” McCormack stated. “Sheep and cattle property. We had no full-time electricity. We had a 32-volt generator that dad would run at night so that a little 12-inch black and white TV could be a thing. This is also when I got my first camera, my hand-me-down camera, and it wasn’t even my dad’s hand-me-down camera. It was my grandfather’s, a Minolta 35mm Mark IV made in either 1949 or 1950. I still have it.”.

His series made it abundantly clear that McCormack cares deeply about nature.

Industry observers note that “My goal here is for people to look at our planet like a Fabergé egg,” McCormack explained. “It is unique, one of them in existence. It’s fragile, it’s intricate, it’s beautiful. It’s something to be protected and taken care of, and it’s something you can fall in love with.”.

It has been revealed that it’s hard to think of a greater loss for Apple than McCormack. It is unlikely that Apple will find someone who is nearly as talented or who cares as much about photography as a fine art. PetaPixel is hard-pressed to believe there was anyone better for his role at the manufacturer than he was.

It measures 4.9 by 3.1 by 2.7 inches, weighs 31 ounces, and is $209.99, down from $279.99. The T99 has seven ports and a rear light that helps with mounting it in dim rooms, and it costs less at $187.49, down from $249.99. Both are 25% off, and SmallRig indicates both recharge in two hours with 100-watt fast charging.

SmallRig rates both batteries IP54, a standard for resistance to dust and splashing water, and lists a drop rating of 4.9 feet for the X99 and 5.9 feet for the T99.

It has been revealed that the Nano36 and Nano72 are mini power banks with USB-C output. Each has a detachable V-mount plate and a threaded hole, so it can mount on a camera cage or rig, or work as an ordinary power bank with the plate removed. Both also have a 27.6-inch USB-C cable that retracts into the body. The 10,000mAh Nano36 delivers up to 45 watts and is $47.19, reduced from $58.99. The 20,000mAh Nano72 delivers up to 100 watts and is $63.99, reduced from $79.99. Both are 20% off. Check the connection and power requirements of the camera, monitor, or light before choosing any of the four.

The two RC lights in the sale are COB video lights. COB, short for chip-on-board, means the LEDs are packed into one small, bright source. Both are about 4.5 inches long and adjust from a warm 2700K to a cool 6500K.

The RC 100B is a 100-watt light with a built-in plate that accepts a V-mount battery, so it can run away from a wall outlet, and it can also be powered over USB-C. SmallRig puts its fan noise at about 26 decibels within 1 meter and says that is quiet enough not to disturb a recording. It is $183.99, down 20% from $229.99. The model on sale is the Standard Version, which does not include a battery.

The RC 60B, sold here as the Mobile Version, has a built-in battery. SmallRig notes it runs for 45 minutes at full power or 75 minutes in its eco mode and keeps working while it charges. It has a 63-watt maximum and comes with a grip handle, a light stand adapter, and a carrying bag. It is $169.15, reduced 15% from $199.

Recent findings suggest that the FL-90 is a 35.4-inch lantern softbox, a globe-shaped diffuser that spreads soft, even light, and it is $60.79, down 20% from $75.99. SmallRig states it opens and collapses in one step. It weighs 1.85 pounds and comes with a skirt that controls where the light spills and a storage bag. It attaches to lights with a Bowens mount, a bayonet fitting common on studio lights. The RC 100B and RC 60B do not have that mount, and SmallRig’s listings say they need the company’s Bowens mount adapter, sold separately, to use a softbox like this one.

Sources indicate that two lights are aimed at close-up work. The RM 03 is a bendable light for macro, or close-up, photography that SmallRig designed for subjects such as mushrooms, plants, and insects. It can wrap around a tree trunk, attach with its clamp, or stand on ground stakes, and it is rated IP54 against rain and dust. It is $39.99, down from $49.99. The RM01 kit is a 2.2-ounce light that SmallRig rates as waterproof. It comes with eight color filters, a diffuser, and a barn door, a set of flaps that narrows the beam. SmallRig suggests it for toy photography, stop motion, and macro. It is $31.99, down from $39.99. Both are 20% off.

Sources indicate that three zoomable flashlights are built to put colored or patterned light on a subject or a background. Each comes with gobos, patterned inserts that shape the beam. The RF 05B produces white light that adjusts from a warm 1900K to a cool 8000K. It weighs 7.6 ounces, is rated IP65 against rain and dust, and costs $31.99, down 20% from $39.99. The 10-watt RF 10C has LEDs in four colors (orange, blue, white, and red) and runs about three hours at full power, according to SmallRig. It drops to $39.99 from $49.99, also 20% off. The 20-watt RF 20C has five colors, and SmallRig suggests it for background and rim lighting, a light from behind that outlines the subject, in portraits at weddings and conventions. It is $67.99, down 15% from $79.99.

The universal phone cage kit, a frame with two side handles for handheld filming, is $47.99, reduced 20% from $59.99. SmallRig claims the two handles add stability for moving shots, and the aluminum cage has mounting points for a microphone and a light. The All-in-One kit comes with an LED light and a microphone, plus a tripod and a power bank holder, and its handles rotate from the sides to the top. SmallRig says it fits phones from 2.52 to 3.46 inches wide. It is $161.49, down 15% from $189.99.

It has been revealed that the selfie monitor kit lets someone filming alone see the frame while using the phone’s rear camera. Its small monitor mirrors the phone’s screen wirelessly from up to 32.8 feet, and a wireless remote triggers the camera. It is $51.99, a 20% discount from $64.99. Read the listing before ordering: SmallRig says the kit is not suitable for Google Pixel phones or the Samsung S22 series, and that with the iPhone’s own camera app it supports 1080p at 60 frames per second, not 4K at 60.

Recent findings suggest that for filters, the 5-in-1 magnetic 67mm kit is $95.99, down 20% from $119.99. Its three filters attach magnetically, so they swap rapidly: a variable ND filter, which darkens the image by an adjustable amount; a circular polarizer, which cuts glare and reflections; and a Black Mist 1/4 filter, which softens highlights. The kit also includes a threaded ring that puts the same filters on a camera lens with a 67mm filter thread. On a phone it needs one of SmallRig’s phone cages and a filter ring that is sold separately, so check the listing for the cage models it fits.

Recent findings suggest that smallRig’s Cage for DJI Osmo Action 6 (Advanced Edition) is a 2.4-ounce aluminum frame with a cold shoe, a slot for mounting a small light or microphone. It snaps on without tools, and SmallRig claims the battery can be changed without taking the cage off. A lens cover and a wrist strap are included. It is $31.99, down 20% from $39.99.

Recent findings suggest that four accessories for DJI’s Osmo Pocket cameras are discounted, and fit differs by model. The auto-deploy mini tripod has the lowest price on the list at $14.44, 15% off $16.99. Its legs open on their own when it is set down, and they are magnetic. SmallRig claims they can hold up to 0.66 pounds on a refrigerator or another surface a magnet sticks to. The magnetic desktop stand tilts and has a magnetic back, a cold shoe, and a plate that fits Arca-type tripod clamps, a common quick-release standard. It is $27.99, down 20% from $34.99. SmallRig lists both for the Pocket 4P, Pocket 4, and Pocket 3. The mini tripod attaches with a standard 1/4-inch screw, which its listing pairs with the Pocket 4 and Pocket 3 handle, so check the mount on a Pocket 4P before ordering.

It has been revealed that two filter kits are listed for the Pocket 4P only. The ND16, ND64, and ND256 kit, which also includes a polarizer and a Black Mist filter, is $39.99, down 20% from $49.99. The variable ND kit is $33.14, reduced 15% from $38.99. ND, or neutral density, filters cut the light reaching the sensor so video can keep a slower shutter speed in bright conditions. The first kit has three fixed strengths that cut four, six, and eight stops of light, and each stop halves the light. The variable filter adjusts from one to five stops for changing conditions. SmallRig says neither kit interferes with the gimbal’s rotation or darkens the corners of the frame.

A cage is a metal frame that wraps a camera body and adds threaded holes for handles, monitors, and microphones. Each is built for one camera model, so match the model name on the listing to the camera.

In a recent development, for the Sony FX5, four HawkLock cages and kits are 20% off. HawkLock is SmallRig’s name for a mounting rail that accessories such as handles slide onto and lock by themselves. The cage on its own is $71.99, down from $89.99, and has a clamp that keeps an HDMI cable from pulling out of the camera. The Advanced HawkLock cage is $95.99, down from $119.99, and SmallRig says its base slides straight into Arca-type tripod clamps and the DJI RS gimbals named on the listing, for quick moves between tripod, gimbal, and handheld shooting.

The kit for the FX5 and its XLR handle has a closed-ring extension that SmallRig claims improves the grip of Sony’s XLR top handle, plus a wrist strap, and is $111.99, down from $139.99. The kit with a top handle and wrist strap has an enclosed top handle that SmallRig says helps prevent drops during low-angle shots. It is $127.99, down from $159.99. XLR is the connector type used by professional microphones. One caution from the listings: the top plate has to come off the cage before Sony’s XLR handle or viewfinder is mounted.

Industry observers note that three Nikon accessories round out the list, each 20% off. The Z6 III cage, $55.99, down from $69.99, locks to the camera at three points, which SmallRig claims stops it from twisting, and its base fits Arca-type tripod clamps and the DJI RS gimbals named on the listing. The ZR cage, $43.99, down from $54.99, has a silicone grip and a clamp that holds HDMI and USB-C cables in place. The L-shaped handgrip for the Z f is a 3.6-ounce silicone grip that SmallRig says gives the camera a more secure hold. It attaches with a thumbscrew, no tools needed, and has a quick-release plate for Arca-type tripod clamps. It is $31.99, down from $39.99.

Recent findings suggest that the SmallRig S70 Ultra-Thin Wireless Microphone has the deepest discount in the sale: 40% off at $53.99, down from $89.99, a saving of $36. SmallRig designed it for content creators, vloggers, and filmmakers who want to record audio without a bulky microphone setup, and claims its thin, discreet design suits interviews, talking-head videos, and on-the-go recording, where keeping the microphone out of sight matters.

Sources indicate that the sale ends November 30, 2026. SmallRig is running the sale at its Amazon U.S. store, the SmallRig official store, and B&H. The prices in this article are the ones SmallRig supplied for Amazon U.S., and the other two stores may differ. The organization also notes that prices and availability may change during the promotion, so check each product page for the current price and stock.
