#57286. Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 21m • 📚 Deep Dive (4282 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hyperallergic ↗ Open Full Page

Is GTA VI the Art Miami Deserves?

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 21 min read (4282 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hyperallergic

⏱️ ~21 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI.
  • The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface.
  • To help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

“Driving at rush hour. SIGNIFICANTLY less cars on the road.” The text was from Miami-based artist, educator, and organizer misael soto, sent yesterday, November 19, a few hours after the release of Grand Theft Auto VI. We’d come full circle: The bumper-to-bumper traffic that Miami, the city I once called home, is now notorious for — in no small part due to overdevelopment, climate change, and strained infrastructure — was being alleviated by a video game that keeps people at home, inside a simulation of the same city locked in time.

The premise of GTA VI is simple on the surface. The game follows Lucía Caminos and Jason Duval in the criminal underworld of Leonida, a fictionalized state based on South Florida: Miami becomes Vice City, the Everglades are the Grassrivers. But its portrayal of real-life hardships, socioeconomic inequality, and even Lucía and Jason’s love story, among other elements, has elicited deeper reflections and responses across our increasingly blurred online and physical worlds.

To help make sense of these tensions, I got on a phone call with soto and Leo Castañeda, two Miami-based artists whose work I admire. Castañeda is an artist and video game designer exploring Latin American Surrealism in the digital age, and soto co-leads Artists for Artists: Miami, which is leading a boycott of Art Basel next month, and works in the overlapping arenas of labor rights, public infrastructure, and conceptual and social practice.

Our conversation was edited and condensed for clarity. I hope you enjoy it.

Left: Leo Castañeda playing GTA VI, with a mural by Ahol Sniffs Glue included in the game. Right: misael soto's selfie in front of the inside of the clock tower in Assisi (photos courtesy the artists).

Hyperallergic: Before we even get into GTA, I was hoping each of you could tell me a little bit about your relationship to Miami — how long you've been there? How do you feel about living there now?

Leo Castañeda: I moved to Miami first when I was 11. My parents first moved to Latest York [from Colombia], and then they thought it was too cold, so they moved to Miami. I went to middle school and high school here, then I moved to New York for college, and I moved back in 2015. When I first moved back after college, it was mostly because of the cost of living in New York. And then, within the 10 years that I've been here, it became the same cost of living as New York, except with Florida salaries.

According to recent reports, I do feel grateful, though, to be part of the Bakehouse Art Complex, where I have an affordable studio. I live in the North Beach area, and I was able to find a sustainable rent. Miami has a lot of arts nonprofits that help over time. I do feel that, as complicated as the Miami arts ecosystem is, it is pretty supportive — but at the same time, it is tied to all the different layers of money that have come in and dominate the arts, which are very present here.

According to recent reports, misael soto: I moved here right after undergrad. I grew up in South Florida, originally from Puerto Rico, and Miami was always la locura, down south. We would visit my cousins and whatnot from time to time. As I became more and more interested in starting my own practice, I moved down here and have continually been sucked back in. I try to leave, and it pulls me back for whatever reason. Since COVID, everything's changed. Miami became the second most expensive city in the country. The influx was palpable: All of a sudden, there were Texas and California and New York license plates, Teslas zipping around town, and rent just started skyrocketing. There's more flooding. But at the same time, it's gorgeous, and it's special. I live in Mid-Beach. I can go to the water, I can breathe in some sea air, I can hear 10 different languages at once.

It's a really complex relationship with Miami. Especially, I think, both of us make complicated art — we both make art that is unconventional and perhaps even, you could say, difficult to collect. I don't know if you describe yourself that way, Leo, but I definitely do. And making this kind of work in a hyper market-driven neoliberal city like Miami, on the one hand, it gives me a lot of fodder, a lot of material, a lot of things to talk about, as we're doing right now. But at the same time, it can be really frustrating and alienating and lonesome, ultimately.

Sources indicate that H: I moved from Argentina to Miami when I was little because my mom got a job there. We lived in the Doral neighborhood, where most people I knew were also from Latin America, until I left for Chicago for college at 18. I've lived in Latest York for over a decade now, but I still feel a strong pull to Miami, I feel seen, surrounded by people whose identities are a bit fractured the way I feel mine is.

According to recent reports, and on the note of nostalgia, GTA is a game that was made over the last 13 years, so it chronicles a Miami that’s partly gone. For example, people say Lucía's home is based on a cute salmon-pink, 13-unit condo in Edgewater that was demolished in 2022 to build a 55-story tower, yet it lives on in the game. What does it mean for a video game to preserve a place that no longer exists?

Sources indicate that LC: Well, a few thoughts. During that 13-year development, I would assume the map design was one of the first things they did. But there are also aspects of the chronicling of Miami, or Miami becoming this satire through the game, that have evolved in a shorter time period. For example, this morning I woke up, and there was a Miami Instagram influencer saying that in the fictional version of the Cuban coffee shop Versailles, which is called Antoinette, the bakery has a sign posted outside that says something like, “any politician must pay for all the food when they leave.” That's a reference from a few years ago, when Trump reportedly went to Versailles, ordered food for everyone, and then didn't pay and just walked out.

So it does seem like a video game takes a long time to make, and this one is probably the most ambitious one ever made — 4,500 people working really, really hard, to the point of even having the union situations that they have in the UK branch of the firm. But at the same time, I feel like they studied Miami extremely well, and the integration with some local businesses and local artists in particular — I've seen a few street artists like Ahol Sniffs Glue, Soak, Tatiana Suarez, Typoe, as well as musician Nick León. One restaurant is based on Juvia on Lincoln Road, which doesn't exist anymore — they got priced out, and now there's a record of it. The game takes so long to make, but it lives in an ever-present, because it doesn't matter if you made an asset 13 years in the past, like Lucía's apartment, or now; they feel like the present. It's an interesting amalgamation. I would have to spend more time with it to really know: Does this feel like Miami in 2014 or Miami in 2026, or a hybrid?

H: To get into the politics of the conversation around GTA, I have a lot of icky feelings about one narrative that's taking hold online, which is that the game is “Woke 3.0,” and that the incels and Trump supporters are pissed about it. I only played for a few hours last night, and I went into a gun shop and bought a shotgun. That, to me, panders much more to the NRA hawks and the pro-gun community than to anything that could be considered woke, you know?

It has been revealed that MS: Hmm. I see it the other way around, actually. To me, it's like pretending in order to pacify, in some ways. It's a very complex thing. On the one hand, I remember seeing the woman twerking on the top of a car as the sun came up over the MacArthur. Now that's in the game. And I remember the “face eater” on the MacArthur. I see a man in a thong skateboarding weekly, and now there's a character like that in the game. I teach art history, and I do a whole week on postmodernism and poststructuralism and simulacrum, and the consequences of that, which I think have led us into some really dangerous flattening territory in terms of the role of the artist in the late 20th to early 21st century. I see this game and the way that it's taken over the city in real life and in gameplay, and it makes me think about how much of this is pacifying the role of the artist, or is it pushing through to the other end and becoming a meta-modernist critique that has some gems in there, if you're willing to find them?

It ultimately makes me feel a bit sad in terms of what we deserve. I texted you yesterday, Valentina, when we were talking about having this conversation, and I mentioned, “Well, maybe this is the kind of art the city deserves.” It's not the art that I want for Miami. But in so many ways, Miami is the perfect place. It's been the city for continual use by image makers, from Hollywood to video games.

Industry observers note that H: There is some talk about the fact that the game does seem to have an awareness and sensitivity around identity. Cygnus, the curator at the Vice City Museum of Art, is the first non-binary character in Grand Theft Auto history. The actor cast for the role, Jesse James Rose, mentioned that to prevent anti-trans violence, GTA made it so players would not be able to harm their character. Does this feel like an honest gesture, though?

It has been revealed that MS: I was just talking to a friend who's been playing it, and she was like, “Where are all the Haitians?” I remembered there was this huge lawsuit against GTA and Vice City, the one set in the ’80s, from about 20 years ago. Haitian groups sued Rockstar over their portrayal. I did some research, and it seems now the tech giant has shifted. They're saying, “We now punch up as opposed to punching down.” That feels, once again, so uncanny in comparison to the ways in which corporate America has shifted. It makes me think of the phrase, “Black faces in high places won't save us.” I don't want to be lobbing grenades at Rockstar. I think it's fantastic that these changes have been made, especially with such an influential game. But at the same time, it feels like the video game, in its attempt to replicate reality, is lagging in this area.

According to recent reports, H: GTA has a long history of racism. We shouldn't forget that Black characters have been associated with criminality throughout all editions of the game. I haven't played enough to say whether that's the case in the latest version. There is also the question of how the organization actually treats its workers, and the labor disputes that are going on behind the scenes. Nestor Uriarte, an animation programmer for Rockstar, wrote an opinion piece for the Guardian where he asked, why is it that with this game that generated billions of dollars, we are still fighting to get union recognition?

MS: I'm curious, Leo, as someone who has been playing games for as long as you have, how you feel about this. I'm a cinephile — I've been one since I was 18, and watched my first Kubrick film the summer before college. And I am dying to see Avengers: Doomsday (2026). I've been following the Marvel Cinematic Universe (MCU) and have been consistently floored by the way they built out this world and the interconnected films. It's history, and it's been making history. But we all know how terrible Disney is. And even with the MCU, they tried to bring in more diversity, and the public didn't respond, so they backtracked on it. I don't know if that analogy holds. But it feels pertinent. It feels similar.

LC: Of course, I have to play more to fully understand it. There's the ads of the game and the game itself. I would say that the Netflix special did feel like it was perpetuating some of the stereotypes of the Haitian community. But at the same time, having played, or seen the range of minority characters so far in the first couple hours, it feels like they have a wide range of personalities, body types, and interests. It's not like they're all criminals. And I also found out that local Haitian muralist Serge Toussaint has his work featured in the game, which I think is an amazing thing. But in terms of artworks in other mediums that really relate to this, this is kind of like, let's say, South Park, or Euphoria — reveals that are a mirror to the world that's very explicitly showing you both the best and the worst, and it's making fun of and critiquing everyone. But then how does it flip to show a latest perspective or a solution?

It has been revealed that I've seen a lot of people, especially women game critics and game developers, celebrating the relationship of Jason and Lucía being a central situation in the game, as opposed to a cast of different men from different backgrounds, or, in GTA IV, the Eastern European guy in the seedy underground. Having the relationship and the cultivating of the relationship be a core mechanic, almost in a Sims-like way — and even the learning of emotional labor, or doing kind things around the house, or the game having a really interesting reward mechanic for the nonviolent interactions ... At least in my experience so far, three hours in, I haven't shot a single shot.

H: Wait, how did you save Donnie in the first mission without shooting people?

Sources indicate that LC: Oh, by hiding. It was saying, “Crouch around to make sure no one sees you.”.

H: I think it's fascinating how different players can make these different decisions. I'm not very good at gaming, so I gave my husband the controller. I was like, “Get us out of here as swiftly as possible. I want to get to Vice City!”.

LC: Yeah, and usually my criticism of Rockstar Games and also Naughty Dog, two massive companies that have these cinematic, movie-like games, is that the story missions often have a path where you fail if you don't take a violent action. The emergent gameplay — which happens just by walking around, the dynamic gameplay that's not in a story mission — is usually extremely layered and nuanced and can go in any direction, violent or not. Again, I'm only three hours in with GTA VI, but so far I appreciate that it is giving the choice of not using violence, and kind of rewarding it. There's something interesting about that. Because usually in those Rockstar games, I'm like, okay, there's this emotional tale, and now there's a mission, and I have to kill 20 minions.

It has been revealed that MS: Leo, I'm thinking about your work and playing your pieces, immersing oneself in these worlds that you create, and there's a kind of mystery in the expansive potential that you create in your installations that at first can be a little overwhelming, but you have to just dive in. And this is the nature of games, or video games. There's a kind of trust fall. And I'm thinking about — let's just go there — the emancipatory potential of that. Because video games, to me, the potential in them as works is the building of awareness, the fostering of empathy, literally embodying someone who has a different way of life or a different body, a different perspective. Especially in our era of political correctness, and a lot of it is warranted, we're asked to speak from our own perspective and not assume things of others. And so this allowance — I wonder how you see the potential in that, especially in something like this game that is so immersive.

LC: I think games as artworks are, to a certain extent, some of the most affordably accessible. Yes, you need to have a PC or PlayStation or Switch or something, but they could be pieces of art that are globally accessible in an immediate way, and they really can affect culture. In terms of empathy, you're controlling a being that you identify as “I”: “I” drove the boat today, or in my game, “I” was camouflaging with the environment to gain energy. There's something there about the mutability of the body, or how one could shift one's self-identity into multiple beings, that is interesting in games, and also interaction and choice as a place that could be art, in a way that performance art also does, and maybe theater. And visual arts in general, maybe in a less touch-based way. But in terms of the empathy, I've been seeing a lot of reviews of GTA VI saying it's actually leading people towards that. Perhaps it is through the romantic relationship [between Jason and Lucía], or maybe by having so much freedom to do whatever you want and kill whoever you want, but then developing these characters and NPCs to a level where they feel like real people.

H: There is one moment in the game that was very emotive in a way that might provoke empathy, and it certainly did for me. At the very beginning — so this is not really a spoiler — we're shown the backstory of how Lucía gets arrested. She's been sitting at a cafe, a little Cuban cafecito, and she's just ordering ice water. The server keeps coming up to her and asking if she wants something else, and she's like, “No, no, just ice water for me.” It's clear that she just can't afford anything else. So in an act of true desperation, and from a place of deep poverty, she decides to rob a payday loan store nearby, and she gets caught. At one point, you can hear the cops saying, “She's saying she left something at the cafe.” And then we see the owners of the coffee shop taking care of her baby, who is then taken by social services.

We're not shown Tomás, her little baby, at the beginning. It's something that the game surprises us with. To me, it was such a thoughtfully articulated moment.

LC: The beginning is so strong. And then having the tutorial on how to walk and use the camera be her nine months later in prison. Out of overcapacity, the prison is letting some people who have lower sentences perhaps have probation, so she's gonna be let go, but the woman who works there indicates she doesn't know if or when Lucía will see her baby again. That works as a narrative tool, a teleology, giving purpose to the game beyond, “Oh, she's just a digital girlfriend.” Now there's this question of what the rewards of behavior are that the game's gonna have when one is part of the criminal underworld, but there is a child in foster care that could be taken back or not. That's gonna be so interesting if that ends up being a fork in the road within the narrative, because many of these games have multiple endings.

In a recent development, MS: This is so fascinating to me in regards to something we were talking about earlier — whether reality is informing the simulacrum and vice versa. It makes me think of how, living in Miami, it continuously feels like maybe the most neoliberal city I've ever lived in. But in so many ways, it oftentimes feels like when you're on the road or when you're at a cafe, you're alone. You really have to fend for yourself in this city. Of course, there are these moments where you break through, or if you're a regular at Enriqueta's, you know who to talk to, this and that. It makes me wonder how the game might change the way that we see ourselves. And, following that thread, how might it actually make us more united?

I don't know if that's a bit of a stretch, but there are just so many people playing this game. And I think over time it's really going to show, as visitors come and reflect their years of gameplay back to the city. In the same way that folks experience Paris syndrome, what will the GTA Miami syndrome be? How might that change us? I was thinking about it for the worse, but how might it change us for the better? Because I don't know a Miami where that childcare situation in the GTA story would happen. Of course, I'm not a caregiver. I'm not a parent. But I don't know that Miami — and I've been here long enough and I have a lot of family here, chosen family. So that makes me, in a weird way, hopeful.

Sources indicate that LC: I think it's interesting, let's say with Pop art and conceptual art — if you use a urinal or a fluorescent light, you think of urinal, Duchamp; fluorescent light, Dan Flavin, etc. These artists are claiming this thing from the world. And it's interesting to have this very fluid cycle of, let's say, the Only in Dade Instagram account becoming almost a live feed of GTA, or us within Miami filtering our experience — when there's a very special or odd moment, it being a rehearsal for the game, or the game getting reflected back in the world.

Industry observers note that if the game is marketing itself as this debauched, wild place, and that lures millions and millions of people in, but then it ends up being this profound story that actually shows how South Florida has challenges of income inequality and climate change ... There's a hurricane system in the game, so there's a very strong chance that there will be flooding. Will that situation, where violence and comedy, or things that are not explicitly telling people what the values should be, actually make them more subtle and implicit? Does that create change or not?

H: We've been speaking over an hour, we could probably talk for two more hours. This feels like a beautiful note to end on. But I want to ask if there are any burning observations you want to share.

Sources indicate that MS: I feel like we should speak about the takeover of Miami in the real world, physically. Anybody trying to do anything — F1, Art Basel, all these people who come in and take over the city, as they've done for decades — if they want to gain favor with locals, just look at what they did with GTA. Because the amount of free advertising — I mean, I went to this GTA VI-themed drag night, and it was not sponsored by them. It was at Las Rosas. They had a pool table and some neons, and they had the beer from the game available for purchase, but the event itself was fully done just to hop on the bandwagon, and everybody was lapping it up. Morphine Love Dion was playing the video game while people were dancing. It layered some uncanny feelings for me. But at the same time, I'm just very, very impressed, and scared, by the power of putting it everywhere to the point where it was inescapable. It's been inescapable for the last week. It's very impressive.

It has been revealed that LC: Yeah. I've met at least two or three people who have been working on some of the release parties. So they're employing local artists and local musicians and local businesses, as opposed to, as misael was saying, these people arriving out of nowhere, renting a place for really exaggerated prices, and not giving back to the local community. At least through employment. We'll see over time if and how it leads to other forms of sustainability locally. I have a photographer friend who, similarly to that drag show, started doing GTA-style photos in front of one of the upcoming signs and probably made some money through that, unofficially. So that's interesting.

It has been revealed that MS: I think there's many ways to be a capitalist, or to do this kind of thing and take over the city in this way. And I've never seen something so thoughtful. It honestly reminds me to some degree of the first couple years of Art Basel, when they would do a lot of public programming and free concerts and they really seduced us ... But that's another conversation. I'll stop there.

H: Well, it's a perfect aperitif for Miami Art Week and the Basel boycott and everything else. And then the G20 summit hosted by Trump in Miami the following week.

H: Yeah, we're going from GTA VI to G20. It's just a perfect pipeline, really.

It has been revealed that MS: It doesn't get any more Miami surreal than that. Truly Vice City.

Tech Report: Student Wrecks Scottish Exhibit in Attempt to Sit on Stone of Destiny

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (241 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A French student who smashed a vitrine protecting the storied Stone of Destiny in Scotland said he did so by right, claiming to having been born in Scotland and thus having been bestowed the privilege of sitting on a relic that had been used to crown Scottish monarchs until the 13th century.
  • Sources indicate that as reported by the BBC, “Arnaud Hercules Harixcalde Logan, 36, pleaded guilty to a charge of maliciously damaging the historic artefact’s glass casing at Perth Museum in July last year.
  • The incident, which forced the closure of the Stone of Destiny exhibit for three months, led to Logan being tackled by a museum visitor and a member of its staff.

A French student who smashed a vitrine protecting the storied Stone of Destiny in Scotland said he did so by right, claiming to having been born in Scotland and thus having been bestowed the privilege of sitting on a relic that had been used to crown Scottish monarchs until the 13th century.

Sources indicate that as reported by the BBC, “Arnaud Hercules Harixcalde Logan, 36, pleaded guilty to a charge of maliciously damaging the historic artefact’s glass casing at Perth Museum in July last year. Perth Sheriff Court was shown CCTV footage which showed Logan using a blue and white hammer to strike the reinforced glass cabinet 24 times—causing £9,000 [around $12,000] worth of damage.”.

The incident, which forced the closure of the Stone of Destiny exhibit for three months, led to Logan being tackled by a museum visitor and a member of its staff. After an initial court appearance last year, the perpetrator fled to Australia and failed to check in with police for several months, as required by law. To that and the smashing incident, Logan pled guilty, with sentencing to follow on January 6.

About the jarring day at the museum, a public prosecutor remarked, “Members of the public appeared distressed and panicked. Staff evacuated everyone from the building. He said he was called Logan and that the Logan clan had been betrayed and that the Stone of Destiny had been stolen from him.”.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A week on from my Adobe MAX 2026 experience, I'm left more conflicted than ever about the democratisation of design.
  • Add Adobe's balls to the wall AI adoption and it feels like we're snowballing into a mass slopathon.
  • MAX made one thing abundantly clear – Adobe is for everyone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A week on from my Adobe MAX 2026 experience, I'm left more conflicted than ever about the democratisation of design. While post-MAX clarity has calmed the excitement of Sneaks and newly introduced Adobe software announcements, an uncertain existentialism still lingers. Finally, everyone has the freedom to create, but in the same breath, oh dear... everyone has the freedom to create.

Add Adobe's balls to the wall AI adoption and it feels like we're snowballing into a mass slopathon. Throughout MAX, I am constantly assured AI is only there for those who want it, but I'm also hyperaware that its siren song is far too tempting for certain creatives. It all boils down to one question. In the age of democratised creativity, what defines real design?

MAX made one thing abundantly clear – Adobe is for everyone. Whether you're a novice creative looking to jazz up a poster, a seasoned influencer wanting clickworthy content or an industry vet trying to adapt to the ever-demanding creative industry, Adobe is, by its own positioning, your best friend.

This is where cracks already begin to form. Classically trained graphic designers, web developers and old-school content creators who learned through education or self-taught graft are left feeling cheated while latest-gen creatives have it all at their fingertips. It's not childish to feel that things are a little unfair. There is value to the blood, sweat and tears of art created over time – something AI appears to extinguish.

Recent findings suggest that and while on the surface, creativity for everyone feels like a utopian dream, the addition of AI makes me worried. Of course, jobs are sacrificed under the guise of saving time and budget, and when everyone can create, where do we find value in creativity?

Industry observers note that can a concept half-baked by a computer hold the same emotional nuance as human-made work? I fall in the camp of no. But art has always been subjective – who's to say an AI-generated design has less value when, at its core, it was sparked by a human idea? A better question is, where do we draw the line?

It has been revealed that it's easy to make Adobe the fall guy for the rise in AI slop, but it's just as much a matter of how we use its tools. At Sneaks, I witnessed a number of genuinely innovative tools, like Project Deep Brush – an AI-powered lighting-aware tool for Photoshop – that proved there's a distinct difference between full-send gen AI and the odd tool to make your everyday workflow a little smoother. Adobe developers aren't sitting in front of an evil AI cauldron preying on the downfall of human design as we know it. Behind the scenes, there are glimmers of hope.

Sources indicate that if used in a measured way, I believe AI tools can be an extension of creativity, but with no constraint other than the moral, and Adobe churning out corner-cutting AI tools with reckless abandon, it's no surprise there's slop everywhere. Latest creatives are hungry to push the confines of what creativity can be – AI is proposed to them as a wacky friend that can do it all. The role of 'creative' is in a state of flux, and with a new generation redefining what creativity means, artistic value has never been more abstract.

Industry observers note that A repeated argument for Adobe's influx of AI innovations was the creative industry's increasing demand for content. A graphic designer may now be expected to be a master of motion design, web development and social media with fewer resources and even less time. These tools are merely a part of evolution – embrace them or get left behind.

According to recent reports, but from the sidelines, I watch in horror as the creative industry eats itself over and over again. More content requires faster output. Faster output is aided by time-saving AI tools. Saved time means more space to create more content to feed the hungry attention economy. We're creating more, but as a result, we're losing a sense of quality and control. And when creativity is democratised, I worry valuable work gets lost in the shuffle.

I worry I'm a snob – that my jaded opinions are stuck in a creative world that no longer exists – but despite my discomfort, I remain hopeful. Creative democracy has its value. Accessibility is better than ever (given you can afford an Adobe subscription), and voices that may not have had the confidence to create are now empowered to do so thanks to Adobe's tools.

According to recent reports, but what of the classic designer, like my father, who has spent decades curating their craft, only to have AI do it in seconds? It's an uncomfortable reality, but change is inevitable. To the jaded, fearful or downright nihilistic creative, I implore you to continue creating on your own terms, whether that means dipping a toe into AI tools or outright denunciation of the technology. Amidst the formulaic sea of AI, it's the quality, human-made content that will be celebrated.

Natalie Fear is Creative Bloq's staff writer. With an eye for trending topics and a passion for internet culture, she brings you the latest in art and design news. Natalie also runs Creative Bloq’s 5 Questions series, spotlighting diverse talent across the creative industries. Outside of work, she loves all things literature and music (although she’s partial to a spot of TikTok brain rot).

Industry News: 15 Van Gogh Masterpieces that Set Auction Records

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2347 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Artnews

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that in 1990 Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr.
  • Below are 15 of the Dutch master’s most remarkable paintings, each of which has achieved a place among the highest prices for a Van Gogh in auction history.
  • A version of this article was first published on May 19, 2026.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that in 1990 Vincent van Gogh’s Portrait of Dr. Gachet stunned the art world when it soared to $82.5 million at Christie’s New York, setting a new record for any painting at auction at the time. It was one of several headline-grabbing sales that cemented Van Gogh as one of the market’s most coveted names. From swirling fields and blazing cypresses painted in Saint-Rémy to delicate still lifes and portraits from Arles and Auvers-sur-l’Oise, Van Gogh’s works continue to captivate collectors and institutions alike. Today his canvases routinely fetch eight-figure sums, driven by their emotional intensity and storied provenance.

Below are 15 of the Dutch master’s most remarkable paintings, each of which has achieved a place among the highest prices for a Van Gogh in auction history.

A version of this article was first published on May 19, 2026. It was last updated on November 20, 2026.

According to recent reports, on May 13, 2021, Christie’s New York auctioned Van Gogh’sBridge at Trinquetaille, completed in June 1888 during his productive Arles period. The painting achieved $37.4 million, including buyer’s premium, surpassing its pre-sale high estimate of $35 million. It depicts the road bridge to Trinquetaille across the Rhône River, near the house where Van Gogh lived for a time with Paul Gauguin. Notably, Van Gogh described the sky and river as “the color of absinthe,” a striking greenish yellow, reflecting his bold palette and emotional intensity. The scene includes figures that the painter called “ruffians of the Rue du bout d’Arles,” referencing the town’s red-light district. After his death, the painting passed through the hands of several owners, including his brother Theo, the British art collector Elizabeth Workman, and Saudi businessman Akram Ojjeh. The painting is currently held in a private collection.

Industry observers note that this work from one of Van Gogh’s celebrated Sunflowers series of 1888 sold for approximately $39.9 million at Christie’s London on March 31, 1987, a record at the time for any painting sold at auction. The buyer was Yasuda Fire & Marine Insurance Co. of Japan (now Sompo), which donated the painting to the Sompo Museum of Art in Tokyo, where it remains today. Executed in vibrant yellows with expressive brushwork, the painting was created to decorate Van Gogh’s house in Arles before a visit by Paul Gauguin, symbolizing the artist’s optimism and creative aspirations during this fertile period in the South of France.

Industry observers note that this canvas, painted in 1890 during Van Gogh’s final months in Auvers-sur-Oise, depicts a seated woman against a backdrop of wheat stalks and poppies. The muted color palette and contemplative mood mark a departure from the artist’s earlier, more turbulent portraits. American casino magnate Stephen A. Wynn made news when he acquired the painting in 1997 for $47.8 million; in 2025 Wynn sold it privately, along with a painting by Paul Gaugin, to hedge fund manager Steven A. Cohen for a combined price of more than $100 million. These private transactions underscore Van Gogh’s enduring prominence and appeal in the art market, particularly for works from the last two years of his life.

On April 24, 1985, Van Gogh’s Landscape with Rising Sun, created in 1889 during his yearlong stay at the Saint-Paul-de-Mausole asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, sold for $9.9 million at Sotheby’s New York. This sale established a record for Impressionist and Post-Impressionist works, exceeding the previous Van Gogh auction high of $5.7 million. The painting portrays a wheat field in the early morning, viewed from the artist’s room on the first floor of the hospital. Before Florence J. Gould purchased it in 1965, the work was owned by physicist J. Robert Oppenheimer, who inherited it from his father Julius, a Viennese collector. The painting was among the earliest Van Gogh works exhibited internationally and was part of the Museum of Modern Art’s first exhibition in 1929. Despite initial doubts about its market appeal, the sale underscored growing enthusiasm for Van Gogh’s landscapes and signaled a turning point in the valuation of his art.

Van Gogh’s Fields near Les Alpilles (1889) sold for $52 million at Christie’s in New York on May 12, 2022. Painted near the asylum at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, the work depicts a wheat field with lilac mountains behind it and a solitary almond tree in its center. The tree’s stark outline suggests Van Gogh’s admiration for Japanese prints. Until the sale, it had long been hidden in private collections, including that of it fashion designer Yves Saint Laurent and his partner Pierre Bergé, who had farmhouses near Saint-Rémy named after Van Gogh. It is rightly celebrated for its vivid brushwork and evocative colors capturing late autumn in the French countryside.

It has been revealed that on November 11, 1987, Sotheby’s New York auctioned Irises, painted in May 1889 within days of Van Gogh’s voluntary admission to the Saint-Rémy-de-Provence asylum. The hammer dropped at $49 million, with a 10 percent commission bringing the total to $53.9 million. The winning bidder turned out to be Australian businessman Alan Bond, who was unable to complete the transaction. The painting was acquired for an undisclosed sum about three years later by the J. Paul Getty Museum in Los Angeles, where it remains today. Previously it had been in the collection of Joan Whitney Payson. Its bold colors and fluid brushwork mark a pivotal moment in Van Gogh’s artistic recovery, reflecting the emotional intensity and renewed vitality he found in nature during his time at the asylum. The dramatic sale drew a packed house and global media attention, cementing the ascendance of Van Gogh as a market titan.

Van Gogh’s Landscape Under a Stormy Sky was painted in April 1889 in Arles and sold for $54 million at Sotheby’s, New York, on November 5, 2015. It was completed a few months after Van Gogh famously mutilated his ear in December 1888 and shortly before he admitted himself to the asylum at Saint-Rémy. The painting depicts a meadow filled with spring flowers, with a man and a woman walking on the left beneath heavy grey clouds. It was one of the last landscapes Van Gogh painted in Arles and is referred to in his letters to his brother Theo in mid-April 1889 as one of six spring studies. The canvas was later retrieved from Arles and sent to Theo in Paris in July. The sky, painted in thick expressive strokes, is unusual in Van Gogh’s Arles work and may reflect the difficult circumstances of his final months there.

On November 4, 2014, Van Gogh’s Still Life, Vase with Daisies and Poppies, completed in June 1890 just weeks before his death, achieved $61.8 million at Sotheby’s Latest York, exceeding its estimate by over $10 million. The artist created this dramatic and colorful canvas while staying at the home of his physician, Dr. Paul Gachet. Garchet was an art collector and amateur painter, and Van Gogh is thought to have drawn inspiration from some of the works in the doctor’s house, including Cezanne’s flower paintings. He may even have given the still life in exchange for treatment.

This rare piece is one of the few Van Gogh paintings sold during his lifetime. It later entered the collection of Conger Goodyear, a founder of the Museum of Modern Art, before moving through private hands and being exhibited at the Albright Knox Art Gallery for over 30 years. The buyer was Chinese billionaire and entertainment mogul Wang Zhongjun, an amateur artist with a fondness for flower-filled compositions. This sale reflects a shift in the Van Gogh market, with East Asian collectors—especially in China.

It has been revealed that van Gogh’s The Avenue of Les Alyscamps was painted in November 1888 during his time in Arles, shortly after his friend Paul Gauguin came to stay with him. The work depicts in vibrant colors the central thoroughfare of the ancient Roman burial ground at Alyscamps, near Arles. It was created during a brief period of collaboration between the two artists, who captured the site, each from different viewpoints. After years in private collections, the painting was sold at Christie’s in Upcoming York on May 12, 2003, for $12 million. When it returned to auction at Sotheby’s New York on November 10, 2015, it fetched $66 million. The buyer was officially anonymous, though believed to be a Chinese collector. This dramatic increase reflects the continuing high demand for Van Gogh’s art.

It has been revealed that completed in 1889 at Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, Wood Cabins Among the Olive Trees and Cypresses showcases Van Gogh’s distinctive impasto technique, depicting two modest buildings in vibrant natural surroundings. This pastoral scene reflects the artist’s deep connection to the Provençal landscape during his prolific asylum period. The painting fetched $71.35 million at Christie’s New York on November 11, 2021, highlighting sustained collector enthusiasm for Van Gogh’s landscapes. Until then, it had been held in the collection of the Texas oilman Edwin Cox.

Recent findings suggest that painted in September 1889 at the asylum in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, this work is one of the few self-portraits in which Van Gogh appears with no facial hair. Created shortly after he shaved his beard, it may have been intended as a gift for his mother to show that he was in better health. The intense blue-green background, combined with his direct, piercing gaze, gives the painting a raw emotional power that distinguishes the artist’s late works. Executed with his signature impasto technique, the canvas reflects both vulnerability and resolve during a fraught period in the artist’s life. It achieved $71.5 million at Christie’s Latest York in November 19, 1998. The work had previously been held in the collection of German entrepreneur Jacques Koerfer and was rarely exhibited, adding to its desirability.

Painted in early September 1889 during Van Gogh’s stay at the asylum of Saint-Paul-de-Mausole in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, Laborer in a Field features a lone peasant working beneath a vast, swirling sky. After a devastating epileptic episode that kept him away from painting for more than six weeks, Van Gogh returned to his brushes with renewed vigor and hope, using the view from his room—a wheat field enclosed by a stone wall—as inspiration. The painting’s earth tones and rhythmic brushwork capture not only its subject’s labor but also the artist’s own struggle toward creative and emotional renewal. This work, painted during one of the most turbulent yet fruitful periods of Van Gogh’s life, sold for $81.3 million at Christie’s Upcoming York on November 13, 2017, having passed through the estate of billionaire collectors Nancy Lee and Perry R. Bass. The painting’s return to the market after decades away attracted strong collector interest, reflecting both its artistic and historical significance.

Completed in Auvers-sur-Oise shortly before Van  Gogh’s death, Portrait of Dr. Gachet (1890) was hammered down for $82.5 million at Sotheby’s Upcoming York on May 16, 1990, setting a world auction record at the time. The buyer was Japanese businessman Ryoei Saito, who claimed he intended to have the painting cremated with him upon his death. This depiction of Dr. Paul Gachet, Van Gogh’s physician, shows him resting his head on one hand, surrounded by foxglove flowers and books. Its emotional intensity and the limited availability of works by the artist made it one of the most coveted Van Gogh portraits ever to appear on the market. After Saito’s death, in 1996, the painting’s whereabouts become uncertain. Reports suggest that it was sold to Austrian-born investment manager Wolfgang Flöttl in 1997 or 1998, but the current owner and location of the painting remain unknown.

Orchard with Cypresses (1888), painted during Van Gogh’s prolific Arles period, sold for $117.2 million at Christie’s Upcoming York on November 10, 2022, setting a record for the artist that still stands. The canvas portrays a vibrant Provençal landscape with twisting olive trees, dark cypresses, and a luminous sky rendered in thick, energetic brushstrokes. Before its record-breaking sale, the work was part of the collection owned by Paul G. Allen, the Microsoft cofounder. Its well-preserved condition, coupled with an exceptional provenance, contributed to its historic result at auction.

According to recent reports, on November 18, 2026, Vincent van Gogh’s Blossoming Chestnut Trees (Châtaigniers en fleurs) (1890), a picture of sunlit trees set against oncoming storm clouds, sold for $190.4 million (including fees) at Sotheby’s. The cover lot for the auction house’s Blaquier-Arrieta collection sale, which the house had billed as “legendary,” it set a newly introduced auction record for the Dutch painter. The reported buyer was dealer William Acquavella.

The artist’s previous record of $117.2 million was set at Christie’s in November 2022 when Orchard with Cypresses (1888), a landscape from the collection of Microsoft cofounder Paul Allen, sold for $102 million. The upcoming result beat that by $73.2 million, a jump of 62.4 percent in just four years.

It has been revealed that that the sale happened at all was a victory for Sotheby’s. Just days before the auction, descendants of Samuel Fischer, the German Jewish publisher who once owned the painting, challenged its sale, arguing that their family had been forced to part with it in Amsterdam in 1936 because of Nazi persecution. Sotheby’s disputed the claim, pointing to archival records showing the painting had sold for 68,000 Swiss francs, around $22,000 at the time, which it considered a fair market price. After several days of talks, the Blaquier-Arrieta family and the Fischer heirs reached an agreement, clearing the painting’s title.

Painted shortly after Van Gogh arrived at Auvers-sur-Oise in May 1890, Blossoming Chestnut Trees is among the 70-plus paintings (and more than 50 drawings) that the artist made there before taking his own life only two months later. It was also one of only eight Auvers landscapes still in private hands, according to research cited by the Art Newspaper.

Sources indicate that the electric scene, with its thick brushwork, also hadn’t been seen in decades. It was last exhibited at the Solomon R. Guggenheim Museum in 1964 before Argentine collectors Carlos Pedro and Nelly Arrieta Blaquier, bought it in 1975—the kind of provenance and scarcity that fuels record-breaking prices like this one.—Daniel Cassady.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that despite the contemporary art world’s increased attention to women’s experiences and the politics of care in its public-facing programming, working mothers employed by London’s galleries and auction houses face widespread discrimination, according to a newly introduced study. As reported by the Art Newspaper today, a survey of 50 employees working in the UK capital’s commercial art sector has found that, for many, having children comes at considerable professional cost.

Industry observers note that the study, conducted by Kate McMillan and Cleo Roberts-Komireddi and published today in the European Journal of Cultural Studies, looked at the extent to which pregnancy and maternity affected career progression among art world workers. Moving beyond previous studies centered on fine artists or senior directors, it focused on lower-paid, non-artist roles such as sales, administration, and marketing. Related Articles Recent Key Departures at Phillips Point to a Pivot in Strategy The Year in Gallery Closures: A Collapse or a Transition to a Smarter Market?

Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s research, which also included 12 in-depth interviews, reveals an industry “marred by implicit and explicit expectations that often result in workers needing to choose between their careers and being parents,” they write. Three quarters of respondents felt that motherhood had impeded career advancement, while 20 percent said they had been explicitly denied promotion.

The authors found poor and sometimes illegal practices across the industry, including employees being “managed” out of their roles while on maternity leave. Such practices, they note, are made possible by a lack of formal human resource structures—only half of the respondence worked for organizations with dedicated HR staff, and just 60 percent said their workplace had a specific parental leave policy. They additionally blamed the art market’s pervasive culture of secrecy.

According to recent reports, class and wealth also play a role in shaping employee experience, the study suggests. For junior employees on modest salaries, the cost of childcare can make travel and attendance at evening events difficult and increase the likelihood of discrimination on the job. At the same time, a lack of resources makes challenging such discrimination daunting, with many women instead choosing to take a less senior position, move into freelance work, or leave the art world.

Roberts-Komireddi and McMillan’s study spanned small galleries to multinational auction houses and found problems across the board. As they say in their report, “A lack of accountability pervades the sector.”.

And you probably know why: it's because then pen he uses in 1995's Goldeneye is presently £6.39 off at Amazon! What's that? The latest James Bond actor has finally been announced? Oh, right. I see. Still, good news about the pen.

Yes, Yes, Robert Pattinson is James Bond, etc. etc. As a fan, I have various thoughts on the matter. But while various brands have reacted to the announcement, we can't say for sure which brands Pattinson's Bond himself will favour. Will he still wear a Tom Ford suit? Will he still wear an Omega watch? And most importantly, will he still write his Christmas cards with a Parker pen?

Pierce Brosnan did – until he clicked the end four times too many and activated the internal grenade. And if you want to make like the '90s Bond and use the same pen (with its explosive features mercifully disabled), it's currently 40% off at Amazon UK, bringing the price down from £16.37 to £9.99.

In the US, meanwhile, the discount isn't quite as generous, but it's still 28% off, down from $19.99 to $14.99.

In a recent development, this stainless steel pen is sleek and classy – it has a chrome trim and a medium point. It offers a smooth writing experience, and an iconic design. Unlike the adapted version from Q-Branch, this one doesn't double as a grenade.

If you're looking for more delectable writing implements, take a look at the most beautiful pens of all time.

Daniel John is Design Editor at Creative Bloq. He reports on the worlds of design, branding and lifestyle tech, and has covered several industry events including Milan Design Week, OFFF Barcelona and Adobe Max in Los Angeles. He has interviewed leaders and designers at brands including Apple, Microsoft and Adobe. Daniel's debut book of short stories and poems was published in 2018, and his comedy newsletter is a Substack Bestseller.

Russian strikes damage historic buildings in Kyiv and Odesa, including World Heritage sites

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multiple heritage sites in Ukraine were damaged by Russian strikes on 19 and 20 November, including the Unesco-listed St Michael’s Golden-Domed Cathedral and Monastery complex and St Volodymyr’s Cathedral in Kyiv, known for its frescoes, as well as 12 cultural heritage sites in Odesa, the strategic port city on the Black Sea, which was hit a day earlier. The entire historic centre of Odesa was added to Unesco’s list of endangered World Heritage sites in 2023.

At least nine people were killed in Kyiv and other regions of Ukraine during the hours-long attack on 20 November.

“Today, Russian drones damaged one of the most famous monuments of our country, the Volodymyr Cathedral,” Tetyana Berezhna, Ukraine’s deputy prime minister for humanitarian policy and minister of culture, wrote in a Facebook post on 19 November after the cathedral in Kyiv was hit, breaking windows and frames and causing “some damage to the paintings and structural elements”.

Sources indicate that the neo-Byzantine St Volodymyr Cathedral, built in the 19th century, is under the jurisdiction of the Orthodox Church of Ukraine (OCU), which broke with the Moscow Patriarchate and was granted autocephaly by Constantinople in 2018. Three of Russia’s most famous artists of the 19th century and early 20th century—Viktor Vasnetsov, Mikhail Vrubel and Mikhail Nesterov—created religious art for St Volodymyr’s, as did the Ukrainian artist Mykola Pymomenko, a teacher of Kazimir Malevich.

Industry observers note that the Austrian embassy, located next-door to St Volodymyr's Cathedral, was also damaged. Kyiv's municipal cultural heritage department published an inventory of damage from the attack, which also includes the embassy of the Netherlands.

A Russian drone was shot down over St Michael’s, which is the headquarters of the OCU, on 19 November.

It has been revealed that berezhna’s post cites the cumulative damage from Russia’s accelerating attacks: “Since the beginning of this year, the number of monuments damaged by Russia has increased by more than a third, and by the end of October it was almost 2,200. Almost 2,700 cultural institutions were also affected.”.

The minister was in Lutsk, a historic city in northwestern Ukraine, this week to strategy for a conference marking the 600th anniversary in 2029 of the Congress of Lutsk, which brought together the regional monarchies of the time. A Russian strike on Lutsk in October damaged Ukraine’s largest painting, Cosmogony, a 2,000 sq. m work by the contemporary artist Petro Antyp.

Sources indicate that unesco has condemned the latest attacks, especially on Odesa, “which hit the centre of the city, within the boundaries of the World Heritage property ‘The Historic Centre of Odesa’” and “reportedly caused damage to several heritage buildings, including the Kalio Palace, a monument of national importance,” according to a statement released by the organisation. The Kalio Palace, built in 1834, is attributed to the Swiss Italian architect Giorgio Torricelli.

According to recent reports, the strikes came amid escalating tensions and a diplomatic chasm that appears to be widening. The Russian President Vladimir Putin mentioned this week that the Kremlin would not negotiate any partial ceasefire or deal with Ukraine after it struck and incapacitated the Kerch Bridge linking mainland Russia to Crimea, a symbol of Russia’s annexation of the Black Sea peninsula in 2014, on 16 and 17 November. At the same time, US President Donald Trump claimed that peace, largely on Russia’s terms, is within reach and reportedly urged European leaders to stop funding weapons for Ukraine. Trump, Putin and the Chinese President Xi Jinping signed a “peace declaration” on 20 November at a trilateral summit hosted by Xi in Shenzhen, China.

In a recent development, A petition to “safeguard Ukraine’s cultural heritage and artistic integrity” was launched last month by the curator Konstantin Akinsha and Bjorn Geldof, the artistic director at Kyiv’s PinchukArtCentre. It calls “for immediate sanctions and the suspension of Russian state participation in international cultural events”. Rapporteur, a Brussels-based policy publication, reported this week that ten European countries are seeking to keep Russia out of the 2027 Architecture Biennale. Russia’s participation in the 2026 Venice Biennale set off a series of protests.

How do artworks acquire value? I discussed this complex question with two New York art dealers during Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America.David Nolan, whose eponymous gallery has been open since 1987, gave the view of an art world veteran; Anton Svyatsky, who opened Management in 2023, provided a newer perspective.

Along the way, we discussed the role of the collector in sustaining value, the challenges of pricing artworks by emerging artists, the ways in which influence and market value have become decoupled, the casino that is the auction house and the zoo that is the art fair.At our talk on Friday, November 13 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, Svyatsky insisted that collectors need to see themselves as responsible for an artist’s value, rather than depend on dealers and institutions for that function. This shift in perspective, and a return to collecting artists in depth, may well be the key to ridding the art world of speculators. Nolan recalled the immense changes that took place during the 1980s, and the increasing attention paid to artworks’ financial value.Speaking of casinos, a flask emerged at the mention of the new partnership between Artnet and Kalshi—you can catch that moment and other choice ones in the video of the talk above.
